title: What do the Detroit Lions need to show vs. the New York Jets?
summary: After a prolonged period of time where everyone had to stew on a tough loss at the hands of the Buffalo Bills in Week 2, the Detroit Lions are back at home this week where they will be hosting the New York Jets. And while the first order of business for Detroit will certainly be […]
full_text: After a prolonged period of time where everyone had to stew on a tough loss at the hands of the Buffalo Bills in Week 2, the Detroit Lions are back at home this week where they will be hosting the New York Jets. And while the first order of business for Detroit will certainly be getting back in the win column, there are facets of the game where a lot of fans will want to see some marked improvement. Whether we are talking communication and cohesion in the secondary, being efficient in the running game, or getting back to bottling up the run as a defense—all of these and more were issues in the loss to Buffalo. However, to play devil’s advocate a bit, the matchup with Buffalo was always going to be tough. By now, you have heard and read it all. Short week after overtime in Week 1, first game in the new stadium for the Bills—you get it. The beauty of forgettable performances like the Lions put on in Week 2 is there is still plenty of football to be played in 2026. Plenty of chances to get better and build on things as a unit. That brings us to today’s question of the day: What area of the game do you most want to see improvement against the Jets? My answer: It has to be the run defense. Offensively, I believe things will only get better as the offense line begins to click as they get more reps with one another. In the secondary, it is a similar story, and the addition of safety Brian Branch in the (hopefully) not-so-distant future would also help immensely. However, they need to get back to what they have hung their hat on since the arrival of coach Dan Campbell and that is being a top-flight run defense. They looked the part against the Saints, but obviously took a step back in Buffalo. The good news is they will have a great opportunity to get back on track against a Jets team that wants to establish the run early and often. Look for the Lions’ defense, led by established All-Pros like defensive end Aidan Hutchinson and linebacker Jack Campbell to set the tone. What about you? What are you most wanting to see in the Lions’ matchup with the Jets? Let us know in the comments below.

full_text: Now that it feels like it has been close to a month since last Thursday, it’s time for the Detroit Lions to get back on that horse in a Week 3 matchup where they will be hosting the New York Jets. As usual, we we set the table by going over some of the changes that the Jets made in the offseason, including bringing in veteran coach Frank Reich as offensive coordinator. They also upgraded their quarterback room by bringing in journeyman quarterback Geno Smith in an effort to unlock a strong group of skill players that includes Garrett Wilson at wide receiver, Breece Hall at running back, and rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq. Flip to the other side of the ball where the Jets like to hang their hat and you will find a front-seven that is stocked with top-end talent. At the edge rusher position alone, they have Kingsley Enagbare, Will McDonald IV, and second overall pick from the 2026 NFL Draft David Bailey. Combine that room with the addition of All-Pro linebacker Demario Davis and you get a potent mix of youth and veteran leadership for the Jets’ defense. After discussing both sides of the ball, we breakdown some key matchups, and give our predictions at the end of the show. You can watch the entire episode right here . title: Lions vs. Jets predictions: 4 keys to victory in Week 3
summary: The Detroit Lions (1-1) and New York Jets (1-1) will square off in a Week 3 battle as coach Dan Campbell welcomes back his protégé, Aaron Glenn, to Ford Field for the first time since the former defensive coordinator left for the Big Apple. “Our players know exactly what’s coming in here because the defensive […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NY - SEPTEMBER 17: Amon-Ra St. Brown #14 of the Detroit Lions runs a route during an NFL game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions (1-1) and New York Jets (1-1) will square off in a Week 3 battle as coach Dan Campbell welcomes back his protégé, Aaron Glenn, to Ford Field for the first time since the former defensive coordinator left for the Big Apple. “Our players know exactly what’s coming in here because the defensive coordinator was here for (four) years,” Campbell said of Glenn and the Jets. “Turn on the tape. … This is not going to be a trap game. This is gonna be a knockout, 60-minute brawl.“ Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Jets in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint. This week’s predictions preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook , who currently have the Lions listed at +1900 to win this year’s Super Bowl and 6.5-point favorites in Week 3 . Jets base schemes For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 3 preview: Breaking down the Jets’ offensive and defensive schemes . Prediction 1: Lions attack forward to offset Jets’ aggressiveness Glenn’s Jets’ defense won’t look like the one he ran in Detroit (the Jets run a 3-4 base with a 2-4 subpackage), but the principles remain the same: Stop the run, press at the line of scrimmage, and take the fight to the offense. On paper, the Jets defense ranks very highly in most statistics (including allowing the fewest yards per game this season with just 197 total ypg), and on film, they fly to the football in both the run and the pass. They plug rushing lanes up the middle with big space occupiers and downhill linebackers, and also have the range to chase laterally down the line of scrimmage. Against the pass, they play press-man coverage at the line, look comfortable in man and zone schemes, and spread out their coverages to the sidelines with their defensive backs. The Jets’ aggressiveness has been a key catalyst in their defensive success in 2026, but this approach also leaves them vulnerable in certain areas. For example, against the run, the Jets ask their defensive tackles to occupy multiple offensive linemen, thus freeing up gap lanes for their linebackers to fill and stop the ball carrier quickly. To offset this, the Lions will need their interior offensive linemen to win one-on-one or run movement-based blocking schemes, such as Duo or pulling guards. Jared Goff will also need to make quick decisions because the Jets defensive line has the fastest “get off” at the snap (0.71 seconds). That being said, their time to pressure is 2.69 seconds (21st in the NFL), meaning that while the Jets have elite quickness, they can get stuck on blocks, creating opportunities for a decisive quarterback. Over two weeks, the Jets’ aggressiveness showed up most when the Titans and/or Packers tried to move laterally with quick screens, passes to the flat, or stretch outside zone runs. The Jets are far too quick and athletic, and New York often chewed up these plays. However, with linebackers attacking downhill, the secondary living in two-high safety shells, and the corners pressing the line, there is often space to operate in the middle of the field. Look for the Lions to be creative with a run-blocking scheme that opens lanes for Gibbs to speed through, and a forward-moving passing approach that attacks the middle of the field with their best skill players, like Amon-Ra St. Brown and Sam LaPorta. Prediction 2: Lots of 11 personnel, keep Jets defense in nickel While Glenn ran a ton of “Base” defense in Detroit and a fair amount during his first year with the Jets, their 2026 approach has seen them play more nickel sets (roughly 77% of the time). While this brings them closer to the league average, their production in Base has been higher. When in a Base defensive set, the Jets have produced impressive numbers, including a -0.58 EPA, best in the NFL. However, when the Jets move to a subpackage look, their production dips, producing a 0.18 EPA and ranking 13th in the NFL. This shows up against both the run and the pass, as they drop from the top of the rankings in Base to the middle of the pack in subpackages. By running a lot of 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR sets), the Lions will not only get their best skill players on the field at the same time, but it will also help lighten the box, set up cleaner rush lanes, and open up opportunities with play-action and in the intermediate passing game. Prediction 3: Lions deploy Base defense to stop the run On the flip side, the Lions will want to stay in their Base defense, especially early in the game, and work to take the Jets’ rushing attack away. NFL teams strive for a balanced run/pass split with their offensive play calls, but the reality is, this is a passing league, and more often than not, teams default to throwing the ball to gain positive yards quickly. Glenn, like Campbell, wants to control the game with the run, and through two weeks, their run/pass split is roughly 44%/56%, resulting in the eighth-highest rushing rate and fourth-most rushing attempts entering Week 3. Despite the dedication to and opportunities in the run game, the Jets are only producing 3.3 yards per rushing attempt (28th) with a -0.20 EPA (28th). One main reason for this lack of production is that their offensive line isn’t getting much push. Most blocking calls are one-on-one matchups where the offensive line is asked to win, or simple inside/outside zone calls, and over two games, New York hasn’t shown much creativity in blocking assignments. As a result, about 30% of their runs gain no positive yardage, and their rushing yards before contact are just 0.76 (24th) as a team, and 0.6 for starting running back Breece Hall. The Jets have shown a dedication to the run, the Lions a dedication to stopping it, and Base defense allows the Lions to get their best run defenders on the field to win this battle in the trenches. Prediction 4: Lions pass rush turns pressures into sacks While the Jets’ run blocking has lacked impact, their pass blocking has been very good, as Jeremy Reisman pointed out in his game observations post; the Jets offensive line currently has PFF’s highest pass-blocking grade (77.4) . In Week 1, the Jets didn’t allow a sack to the Titans, and while they did give up four sacks to the Packers, many were coverage-based rather than pressure getting home, as shown by their time-to-pressure allowed numbers (2.76 seconds, 13th in the NFL). However, the Jets have surrendered 33 pressures through two games (28th), indicating a few things. First, quarterback Geno Smith is holding onto the ball (he averages 2.97 seconds per throw, 7th longest), and his line is holding up just long enough to keep him upright. Second, Smith still has enough mobility (at 35 years old) to stretch his time in the pocket. And lastly, neither the Titans nor the Packers could consistently generate a pass rush that could finish. Bottom line, the Jets’ offensive line and veteran quarterback have felt some heat, but have mitigated that pressure for the most part. If the Lions want to disrupt the Jets’ success, they’ll need to turn those pressures into sacks. For this to happen, the Lions will need to keep their aggressive approach on the defensive line, deploying stunts and pulls and continuing to generate pressure at a high rate. Through two games, the Lions’ time to pressure is 2.51 seconds (sixth fastest in the NFL), resulting in 39 pressures (fifth most in the NFL) and seven sacks (fourth). Entering Week 3, Aidan Hutchinson ranks third in the NFL in pressures (14) and sacks (3), but he’ll need help from his other starting defensive linemen: DJ Wonnum (six pressures, no sacks), Alim McNeill (four pressures, one sack), and Tyleik Williams (four…

title: Detroit Lions vs. New York Jets preview, prediction: On Paper
summary: The Detroit Lions are looking for a rebound this Sunday after a pretty sound defeat at the hands of the Buffalo Bills. Prior to the start of the 2026 season, Week 3 against a New York Jets team that finished 3-14 last year looked like an easy win. But Aaron Glenn has the Jets inches […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 13: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions celebrates after scoring a touchdown with Jared Goff #16 against the New Orleans Saints during the third quarter of the game at Ford Field on September 13, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Mike Mulholland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions are looking for a rebound this Sunday after a pretty sound defeat at the hands of the Buffalo Bills. Prior to the start of the 2026 season, Week 3 against a New York Jets team that finished 3-14 last year looked like an easy win. But Aaron Glenn has the Jets inches away from a 2-0 start this year. Is that start a mirage, or are the Jets truly a formidable foe this year? Let’s take a closer look in our Lions vs. Jets Week 3 preview and prediction. It’s “On Paper” time. Note: This is the last week we’ll be using any 2025 data. Lions pass offense (13th in DVOA) vs. Jets pass defense (4th) 2025 rankings: Lions pass offense (6th) vs. Jets pass defense (32nd) Week 1 (Saints): 204 passing yards, 96.7 passer rating Week 2 (Bills): 289 passing yards, 130.0 passer rating It took a while for things to get going, but Jared Goff and the Lions’ passing offense finally looked like itself in the second half of the Bills game. Is that a legitimate data point or did the Bills play Detroit differently while up two or three scores? It’s a very fair question to ask, and one that probably will keep my confidence in this unit at “cautiously optimistic” until we get more information. So far this year, the Lions rank: 22nd in yards per attempt (6.9) Fifth in passer rating (113.2) Fifth in dropback EPA (0.270) 10th in dropback success rate (49.4%) I see no reason to believe this can’t be a top-10 passing attack yet again, although there was one significant step back last week: pass protection. Last week, the Bills produced 29 pressures, according to PFF, and four sacks on 42 dropbacks. Detroit now has the 27th ranked pass blocking grade by PFF, although they oddly rank eighth in ESPN’s pass block win rate. The good news is that the biggest culprits of last week’s protection breakdowns were backups. Right tackle Larry Borom allowed 11 pressures vs. the Bills, and left guard Ben Bartch wasn’t far behind with six. Both of those players are expected to go back to the bench this week with Blake Miller and Christian Mahogany on track to return. Week 1 (Titans): 127 passing yards allowed, 80.2 passer rating Week 2 (Packers): 136 passing yards allowed, 91.9 passer rating Last year, the Jets were an absolutely awful passing defense, ranking in the bottom 10 of most statistical categories, including passer rating allowed (110.9, 32nd), yards per attempt (7.5, 25th), dropback EPA (29th), and DVOA (32nd). This year is off to a much more promising start, although they’ve done it against a Titans passing offense that was bottom three last year, and against a Packers team in the rain with no offensive line. Still, the stats are impressive. The Jets pass defense ranks: Second in yards per attempt (4.7) 12th in passer rating (85.8) 11th in dropback EPA (-0.051) 6th in dropback success rate (39.7%) The highlight of their pass defense is their pass rush. Led by rookie and second overall pick David Bailey (2.0 sacks, eight pressures), the Jets have produced an 8.5% sack rate on dropbacks (fifth highest), despite the fact that their pressure rate is just 36.6% (16th). They’re selectively aggressive, sporting just a 23.9% blitz rate (23rd), but that jumps to 28.6% on third down (18th). Their secondary is full of a rag-tag group, but 2025 third-round pick Azareye’h Thomas is playing quite well (77.2 PFF grade, eighth among CBs). Player to watch: Bailey vs. Miller. Bailey has insane speed to deal with (4.50) and Miller is dealing with a knee injury. Not an ideal matchup for Detroit, but it’ll be a good, early test for both rookies. Advantage: Lions +1.5. Maybe I’m being too dismissive of the Jets after watching the Packers get run out of their own house against the Falcons, but I’m just not quite buying that significant of a turnaround for the Jets defense. They’ve yet to really be tested, while the Lions passing offense can be trusted after years of consistently top-10 play. Protection should be better this week, which should help Detroit get off to a faster start. Lions run offense (4th) vs. Jets run defense (1st) 2025 rankings: Lions run offense (10th) vs. Jets run defense (16th) Week 1 (Saints): 165 rushing yards, 5.0 YPC Week 2 (Bills): 66 rushing yards, 3.3 YPC I find it a bit odd that the Lions’ run offense DVOA is ranked so high because that isn’t matching any other statistical benchmarks. They currently rank: 10th in YPC (4.4) 15th in rush EPA (-0.133) 10th in rush success rate (43.6%) Obviously last week was a significant step back, but Detroit was harmed by a beat-up offensive line and an abandonment of the game script when they were down 21-0 early in the game. The signs of a revamped rushing game are still there, but I’m still a bit skeptical of whether they’re truly a top-10 unit yet. There are good signs—they rank 11th in yards before contact per carry and t-fourth in 10+ yard rushes—but there are also discouraging signs, like their third-highest “stuffed” rate (rushes that earn 0 or fewer yards). Still, Jahmyr Gibbs is the ultimate equalizer, and he currently ranks fifth in rushing yards after contact (131). Week 1 (Titans): 68 rushing yards allowed, 4.9 YPC Week 2 (Packers): 63 rushing yards allowed, 3.5 YPC Again, it feels like we have very little information to go off of here. The Jets have only allowed 131 rushing yards thus far (fewest), but they’ve also faced the fewest rushing attempts, in just 32. The Packers may have the worst rushing attack in football right now, and the Titans actually ran the ball fairly effectively against the Jets (+0.11 EPA/rush, sixth-best in Week 1), but only rushed 14 times. So I’m more inclined to go off of last year’s numbers, which were pretty average: 21st in yards per carry allowed (4.4) 25th in rush EPA (-0.034) 17th in success rate (41.4%) That said, the Jets made some significant offseason moves to improve upon that unit, including trading for 360-pound defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat and signing veteran linebacker Demario Davis. Both have made a significant and noticeable difference. Player to watch: Sweat. Amongst interior defenders, Sweat ranks 19th with a 70.3 PFF run defense grade. That’ll be a serious test for Detroit’s up-and-down interior offensive line. Advantage: Draw. My gut tells me the Lions could get things going again with a healthy offensive line, but there’s just not enough data for me to feel any level of confidence there. Both the Jets and Lions look improved from last year, but there’s enough noise in the early data for me to be skeptical. Jets pass offense (8th) vs. Lions pass defense (19th) 2025 rankings: Jets pass offense (31st) vs. Lions pass defense (6th) Week 1 (Titans): 215 passing yards, 104.0 passer rating Week 2 (Packers): 218 passing yards, 90.2 passer rating The Jets were not just the worst passing offense in football for the 2025 season, it was one of the worst attacks in years. Unfortunately for Lions fans, I’m not sure how much we can look into last year’s data. The Jets made changes at offensive coordinator, quarterback, and added a handful of weapons this offseason, and it’s off to a somewhat promising start. It begins with Geno Smith, who is coming off a terrible year in Las Vegas, but has provided at least some stability in New York thus far. So far, the Jets passing offense ranks: 15th in yards per attempt (7.1) 15th in passer rating (95.8) Ninth in dropback EPA (0.205) 12th in success rate (48.1%) The biggest key to the Jets’ success has been pass protection. title: The Packer Situation is Apocalyptic
summary: It’s easy to overreact to a small sample of three games, but I don’t think the title of this post is an overreaction. One of the reasons I don’t think it’s an overreaction is that I still believe the Green Bay Packers have a high number of extremely talented players on their team. I do […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s easy to overreact to a small sample of three games, but I don’t think the title of this post is an overreaction. One of the reasons I don’t think it’s an overreaction is that I still believe the Green Bay Packers have a high number of extremely talented players on their team. I do not think this is just a team of bums. However, I also think that doesn’t matter because they have an unfixable, massive problem on the offensive line, and specifically the interior (though the tackles are no great shakes either). When I’m projecting a team’s fortunes for the year, there is, in the back of my mind, a sort of “worst-case scenario” status I think about on every position group that is aligned with the concept of the “replacement player.” The replacement player is a baseball concept which sets the baseline for production as “the best guy you can acquire freely right now in a pinch.” Basically, the best guy not on any team. Philosophically speaking, you should not have players worse than that guy on your team, and certainly not starting for you, which brings us to this. According to NextGenStats, the Falcons defense recorded 15 quick pressures vs Green Bay tonight, 2nd most on any game this season. The most was 17—which the Vikings defense put up against Green Bay. — Mina Kimes (@minakimes.bsky.social) 2026-09-25T03:37:48.104Z and this: Our tracking has Green Bay's OL winning in pass protection on just 16% of dropbacks (worst in the NFL by a mile). To put that in perspective, the average is close to 50%. Not great Bob. https://t.co/6ZxCUx9e5X — Mina Kimes (@minakimes) September 25, 2026 The problem, and excuse the yelling, is that YOU’RE NOT SUPPOSED TO HAVE A POSITION GROUP THAT CAN POSSIBLY BE THIS BAD. If there was just one weak link on the line, that would be something. If the Packers had successfully drafted for offensive line depth over the past several seasons, maybe they could weather this, but they just can’t. It’s impossible. Most of their monetary capital is tied up in Zach Bako-Bewele , who may never play again after a full patellar tendon tear. They also gave a lot of money to Aaron Banks, who is both injury-prone and terrible. In terms of draft capital, Anthony Belton is a former second-rounder and appears to be terrible. The shining star of the group, Jordan Morgan, appears to be “maybe ok.” I’m not even entirely sure what Sean Rhyan is yet, but no one is approaching average. You cannot spend this much on a position and be this bad at the position. It’s almost not possible, and it’s made worse by pure depth backups like Donovan Jennings and Jacob Monk offering nothing. I don’t expect much from late-round picks and afterthought free agents, but some base level of competence would be nice. You should not employ football players with no ability to play football! The only rational move right now is to fire Luke Butkus, the incompetent offensive line coach who may very well be a sleeper agent. Or maybe it’s just that his dad used to eat meat grilled on burning newspaper . Anyway, these players may all be terrible, but it’s also clear that no one has taught them to be anything other than terrible. If I were a position coach and my guys put up stats that said they were three times worse than the worst unit and also maybe one of the worst of all time, I would expect to not work there anymore. There are no new players to hire; the only choice is to teach these losers to play better. Or, alternatively, to just laugh at what we’ve become, accept our fate, and move on. I’ve never seen anything like this outside of an expansion team. There is a real risk they turn Jordan Love into David Carr/Tim Couch at this point, and some grown-up in the room needs to put a stop to it.

title: Packers Discussion: How would you fix the offensive line?
summary: Unfortunately, this might end up being a weekly post at this point. Real simple question: How would you fix the Green Bay Packers’ offensive line? Personally, I don’t think the team is going to make a coaching change in-season. I also don’t really think that a short-term free agent addition fixes what is going to […]
full_text: (Photo by Chris Leduc/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Unfortunately, this might end up being a weekly post at this point. Real simple question: How would you fix the Green Bay Packers’ offensive line? Personally, I don’t think the team is going to make a coaching change in-season. I also don’t really think that a short-term free agent addition fixes what is going to be a long-term issue for the Packers. The way I see it, the only way out is through. According to Over the Cap , the Packers are effectively $11 million over the cap in 2027, despite only having 44 players under contract. Because of how young the Zach Bako-Bewele contract is and the fact that Aaron Banks’ contract is how the team borrowed cap space for this year, even if the team moves on from those two players next off-season — it will likely come from post-June 1st designated releases, meaning that they’ll see little cap relief from those moves until after the draft. In short, the long-term timeline of the club was leveraged for the 2025 and 2026 seasons, which haven’t exactly gone great — if you haven’t noticed. There isn’t going to be a ton of money to go around for outside additions, even in 2027. On top of that, two offensive linemen that fans wanted to run out of town after performing poorly last season, left tackle Rasheed Walker and center Elgton Jenkins, are both playing better for new teams in 2026. That’s only going to add fuel to the fire that this is a coaching problem on the offensive line, not necessarily a talent problem. The volume of mental mistakes on the line (really, the team in general; just go look at the Packers’ penalty numbers overall) compounds that. Ultimately, Green Bay needs these young offensive linemen to perform, because help isn’t going to come until after they pull the plug and decide to pay down their cap debt — which will take at least one season but could take multiple, depending on how long and hard they decide to push during this “window.” I believe what we’re going to see for the remainder of the season is the team trying to make it work with what they have internally, because it’s the only thing that matters long term. If the coaching staff can’t produce improvements, expect some heads to roll after the season. It’s going to be easier to sell “a new coach can come in and fix this line” than “we can add a brand new offensive line” in the context of the team’s cap and draft pick situation. Hopefully, we can keep our quarterback healthy until then. — Update: Alright, I watched the offensive film (ask me about defense tomorrow; I’m clocking out). Assorted thoughts: On the 4th and 1 at the goal line Rhyan blows a block and the DT doesn't even think about playing the run, goes straight to Jordan. If DL aren't thinking run in short yardage at the goal line, you're fucked beyond belief. Get Monk off the field and run gap so you can do anything https://t.co/p3QUVC1xMv pic.twitter.com/SU7lPIXbwX — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 25, 2026 Atlanta didn’t even respect our run game in short-yardage goal-line looks. They can’t live off screens and short passing being their “run game” if they want to do anything in the red area. That and because they can kind of get knockback right now (look at the Belton/Redman downblock combo to the Mike, Burton/Morgan fitting on pulls well) https://t.co/wpYzvOoR0m pic.twitter.com/XTmefftJeN — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 25, 2026 Anthony Belton is still a people mover (see clip above), but he can’t hang in pass protection at tackle when he’s going against wider edges who build up steam before the point of contact. He’s a guard playing tackle. The coaching staff needs to fix this. What does that mean at right tackle? No idea. Play Travis Glover and/or John Williams next game and see if you have an answer there. If not, the team should honestly make a move for the sake of ensuring that Jordan Love doesn’t have a season-ending injury that could impact 2027, too. He’s taking far too many hits right now. Jager Burton played poorly, but he doesn’t look physically overmatched like Jacob Monk. Monk is a backup center playing starting guard. This cannot continue. I don’t care how nice of a guy he is in the locker room. No one blocks the nose tackle. No one blocks the Mike. They miss the stunt play-side despite four hands getting on it. No one knows what the hell they're supposed to be doing https://t.co/dH5q2ZEyjM pic.twitter.com/UVGtMFVKPy — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 25, 2026 The offensive line looks really poorly coached. Tons of confusion up front. It gets worse when the team is trying to run zone runs, because there are a lot more rules and a lot less “just knock the guy off the ball.” When the team is doing gap runs (like that Belton clip two links above), things are much better. They probably need to scrap their training camp plan of being a zone/bootleg team. They’re simply not good enough at coaching the rules. They can’t ever completely abandon the run game like they did last night. TL;DR: Morgan-Banks-Rhyan-Belton-Glover/Williams left to right until both Glover and Williams have failed. If they both fail, find a right tackle before the trade deadline. If I were Gute, I might cut Monk just so they can’t use him at guard again. Donovan Jennings hasn’t been much better, either. Get into gap scheme runs because this is what this offensive line can do, even if the coaching staff wanted to run zone. They aren’t good enough at coaching zone runs for it to work. title: How Matt LaFleur stacks up to other coaches at the end of their Packers tenure
summary: Since Vince Lombardi left the Packers’ sidelines, 10 different men have been the head coach of the Green Bay Packers. Of those, only two have one titles, and all of their tenures have ended badly. This isn’t surprising. The Tom Cruise quote from Cocktail is accurate: everything ends badly, otherwise it would never end. Of […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Head coach Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers looks to throw the red flag against the Atlanta Falcons during the first quarter of the game at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Since Vince Lombardi left the Packers’ sidelines, 10 different men have been the head coach of the Green Bay Packers. Of those, only two have one titles, and all of their tenures have ended badly. This isn’t surprising. The Tom Cruise quote from Cocktail is accurate: everything ends badly, otherwise it would never end. Of course, Matt LaFleur’s tenure hasn’t ended yet, but it might be in the process of ending. How does it compare to those who have gone before him? For starters, LaFleur is on a nearly unprecedented championship dry streak. I’ve pointed this out before, but it bears repeating: with eight seasons (or at least, seven full seasons and one partial one) under his belt, LaFleur is tied with Bart Starr as the longest tenured Packers coach to never win a title. And I think Bart Starr gets some leeway there because of, you know, all the titles he won as a player. It didn’t make him a better coach, but you could at least see the appeal of having a guy with five NFL championships around. But statistically, LaFleur doesn’t stack up much better. Via data from Pro Football Reference, I compared LaFleur to the other nine post-Lombardi coaches in Green Bay, seeing how they stacked up statistically across the first three games of what would become their final seasons. PFR had worthwhile data for 14 different categories: wins, points scored, points allowed, first downs gained, total offensive yards, total passing yards, total rushing yards, turnovers, first downs allowed, total yards allowed, passing yards allowed, rushing yards allowed, takeaways, and penalties. Are all of those the head coach’s problem? Not really, no. But the buck has to stop somewhere, and head coach is a “get hired to get fired” job; sooner or later, you’re responsible for the whole team’s performance. An offensive coach will be on the hook for the defense’s failures one way or another, in part because he’s the guy who hires the defensive coordinator. In those 14 categories, LaFleur ranks worst in three categories: points allowed, rushing yards, and penalties. I find these three to be particularly damning. For starters, points allowed is, in many cases, an offensive stat. If your offense either turns the ball over deep in its own territory or can’t stay on the field long enough to give the defense a breather, the defense is going to get gashed and gassed, alternatively. And both have happened to the Packers. In Week 1, turnovers by the Packers’ offense deep in its own territory set the Vikings up with touchdown drives of just one and 14 yards. 15 yards of offense for two touchdowns. Must be nice! The Vikings also cashed in a 28-yard drive for a touchdown after the Packers’ special teams allowed a big kickoff return. And in Week 2, a fumble deep in Packers’ territory also set up the Jets for an easy field goal after advancing just four yards. Points allowed, I think you’ll agree, is not always a solely defensive stat. Then, just last night, we saw the result of an offense that couldn’t stay on the field. The Packers possessed the ball 10 times in their Thursday Night Football debacle against the Atlanta Falcons, but on five of those drives they ran four plays or fewer. That includes a four-play drive that was only technically four plays; the fourth was a blocked field goal, which goes down as an offensive play for charting purposes. So really, it was five three-and-out drives for the Packers, which put their defense back out on the field again and again with predictable results. Bijan Robinson glided through a gassed Packers’ defense like they were on skates. They might as well have been. Points allowed, again, is not always a defensive stat. The rushing yardage figure is another bad look for LaFleur if only because it’s a breakdown of his core philosophy. The “Matt LaFleur has a run-first offense” take has always been kind of a farce; few NFL teams actually pass more than they run, and LaFleur’s offenses have always been pretty efficient in the passing game. But by reputation, LaFleur’s supposed to have a good ground game. In 2026, he doesn’t, and of the 10 post-Lombardi coaches, nobody has produced fewer yards on the ground than LaFleur’s Packers this year. He doesn’t have a ground game in part because he got caught in a schematic shift that didn’t work. During his seven-plus years with the Packers, LaFleur has gradually transitioned from his original wide zone run scheme to a more gap-based ground game. The Packers invested heavily in this transition in 2024 and 2025, signing inside power runner Josh Jacobs and massive offensive lineman Aaron Banks, supposedly a road grader on the ground, while drafting Anthony Belton, another massive lineman who supposedly could move bodies on the ground. Jacobs has been the best of those three, but in 2026 he’s nowhere to be found — much like Banks, I suppose. Belton, meanwhile, has never found a home on the offensive line and hasn’t looked comfortable wherever the Packers have put him, leading to cascading failures on the offensive line and, as a result, a bad running game. Then there’s the penalties. I saw all the iffy ones in Week 1, just like you, but’s more than that. It’d be one thing if there were just one bad game of penalties, but through three weeks LaFleur’s team has been penalized 32 times. None of the other post-Lombardi coaches were penalized more than 28 times in the first three games of their final year. LaFleur’s predecessor, Mike McCarthy, who had supposedly lost control of the locker room and the team discipline that goes with that, only saw his team earn 15 penalties during the first three games of 2018. Maybe LaFleur somehow turns things around. Maybe I’ll get a check in the mail for a million dollars. Stranger things have happened! But compared to the final year of every other head coach whose time ended in Green Bay, LaFleur is looking pretty bad. Maybe he makes it out of this year without getting fired, but the evidence shows better coaches than LaFleur didn’t make it to the next season after an abysmal start.

title: Packers Film Room: Building off Dash
summary: Over the first couple of weeks of the season, we’ve seen the Green Bay Packers working Dash motion into their offense. It’s been primarily used in one specific way in the run game. We talked about that last week, but let’s show it again here. “Dash” involves a TE arcing back in motion before the […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Over the first couple of weeks of the season, we’ve seen the Green Bay Packers working Dash motion into their offense. It’s been primarily used in one specific way in the run game. We talked about that last week, but let’s show it again here. “Dash” involves a TE arcing back in motion before the snap. At the snap, he fires toward the line. The Packers have used this motion to get to a power run the vast majority of the time: the Dash motion man kicks out the EMOL (End Man on Line) and the guard from the motion side pulls as a G Lead. We have seen slight variations to this, but nothing major. Backside pass tags as an option if the defense is caught in a certain look or blitz. In Week 1, we saw Matthew Golden get a 1st down off a backside slant against a blitzing defender . In Week 2, we saw Matthew Golden catching a big pass off a Bubble to set up the game-winning field goal in overtime . Both of those were merely slight variations on a theme. This week, we saw it open up a bit. It’s the Packers’ first drive of the 2nd half. They’re down 17-7, facing 1st & 10 at the 50-yard line. They come out in 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR), which is how they like to run their power concept. They’re in a 2×2 condensed look, with a TE in-line on either side of the line. Before the snap, Josh Whyle [81] goes in Dash motion, looping 4 yards behind Jordan Love [10]. At the snap, Wyle releases toward the line, looking like he’s kicking out the EMOL. This forces a reaction from Divine Deablo [0], the linebacker to that side of the field. He drives down hard at the point of attack to take away the run. But it’s all a ruse. Whyle releases through the line, angling toward the sideline (he doesn’t get to the sideline because Deablo kicks out a foot and takes Whyle down). Christian Watson [9] is the receiver to that side, and he pushes hard vertically down the field. The Falcons are in a two-high look with their safeties, with the safety over Watson backpedaling against the vertical push from Watson. Watson puts on the brakes 15 yards down the field. With the safety pushed back and Deablo at the line to attack the run, there’s a nice open space for Watson to settle into. Love hits Watson, who turns upfield to pick up a few more yards. By the time the whistle blows, it’s a 22 yard gain. Nice way to build off a concept you’ve shown a decent amount of through 2 weeks (and have had success with). I’ve been waiting for some vertical variations off that motion, and it looks like we’re starting to get them. I’m looking forward to seeing what else they do with this. title: Packers Film Room: Long snapping on kicks in Week 3
summary: In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We only have 3 that we’re looking at this week, but we get an interesting look from the Falcons field goal block unit that we’ll take a slightly deeper look at. But, for starters, how was the snap location this […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We only have 3 that we’re looking at this week, but we get an interesting look from the Falcons field goal block unit that we’ll take a slightly deeper look at. But, for starters, how was the snap location this week? Pretty good this week. All 3 snaps solidly in the green. The only one that was over the spot of the hold was actually the field goal attempt that was blocked. Kick 1: Extra Point (Made) Snap to the body. Clean catch. Clean hold. Smack knocks it through. Kick 2: 47 yard Field Goal (Blocked) We’ll watch the video first. As I mentioned, snap is clean over the hold point. Clean hold. You want the operation to take 1.3 seconds and the Packers were right on that (I have it at 1.34, but my stopwatch skills are not always to be trusted). We’re gonna keep an eye on these three guys: On the first attempt, it was just a pure power move by that group of dudes. Jacob Monk [62] and Anthony Belton [71] got low and blocked down. They looked to do the same thing this time. Monk never gets out of his stance which seems like a problem overall, but, for this block, it didn’t really make a difference. The inside man loops to the other side, crossing the face of Matt Orzech. The middle man drops out. The outside man swims over Belton’s outside shoulder. With Jonathan Ford and Barryn Sorrell blocking out and Belton blocking down, it’s a free lane for Zach Harrison [96], who gets his hand up for the block. Belton has his arm out to try to slow the path of Harrison, but Harrison runs right through it. Kick 3: Extra Point (Made) After all that, this last one is pretty straightforward. Snap is to the body. Clean hold, Smack knocks it through. Harrison tries to swim past Belton again, but this time Belton gets a little higher and his arm is in a better position to slow Harrison. Even then, Harrison seems to nearly get a hand on it. Albums listened to: Karina Rykman – Late Checkout

title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers fans must free themselves
summary: When I take the chair as Curds author once a week, I usually keep the fourth wall up. This is a news roundup series. Readers come here for links to the latest stories about the Green Bay Packers, with a light sprinkling of analysis and opinion. But it’s hard to keep up appearances after sleeping […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - AUGUST 02: Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFluer waives to fans during the annual Green Bay Packers Family night practice at Lambeau Field on August 2nd, 2025 in Green Bay, WI. (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images When I take the chair as Curds author once a week, I usually keep the fourth wall up. This is a news roundup series. Readers come here for links to the latest stories about the Green Bay Packers, with a light sprinkling of analysis and opinion. But it’s hard to keep up appearances after sleeping on that embarrassing loss the Packers suffered to the Falcons last night with the whole world watching. I host a weekly in-season podcast about my favorite team, and a common tongue-in-cheek refrain I use on that show is this: Free yourself from the burden of expectations. Well, folks, let me tell you. There has never been a better time to do just that. This team is bad right now, and few of the problems just aren’t fixable in-season. Free yourself from the burden of expectations. The offensive line is a mess. ZBB is lost for the year. The unit is green and poorly coached. Some guys are out of position. Some of them just aren’t very good. And help is not on the way. Free yourself from the burden of expectations. Between the offensive line and this current stable of backs, the running game is historically bad. Josh Jacobs, if he ever comes back, is not saving the run game. Free yourself from the burden of expectations. Jordan Love is an excellent player. But he’s going to look bad, get hit, and possibly even hurt, because opposing defenses have precisely zero respect for the run game. Free yourself from the burden of expectations. Jonathan Gannon’s new-look Packers defense is actually interesting and, I think, deserves optimism overall. But they’re not going to win every week, and Micah Parsons may only improve that slightly. Free yourself from the burden of expectations. It’s going to be a long season, so I suggest fans steel themselves against anguish and accept that this year’s Green Bay Packers are going to be hard to watch. Packers report card: Lots of F’s As you might expect from a 35-14 loss, it’s nothing but bad grades for the Green Bay Packers. Just how bad? title: Houston Texans Prediction at Colts Week Three
summary: The Texans unfortunately enter familiar territory. For the second straight year and third time in the DeMeco Ryans era, the Texans are 0-2 out of the gate. They face their AFC South rivals the Indianapolis Colts (0-2), who’ve also tripped coming out of the gate. Both teams are exceptionally desperate for a win, and neither […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - JANUARY 04: Running back Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts is tackled by a swarm of Houston Texans defenders during the NFL game between Houston Texans and Indianapolis Colts on January 4, 2026, at NRG Stadium in Houston, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Texans unfortunately enter familiar territory. For the second straight year and third time in the DeMeco Ryans era, the Texans are 0-2 out of the gate. They face their AFC South rivals the Indianapolis Colts (0-2), who’ve also tripped coming out of the gate. Both teams are exceptionally desperate for a win, and neither are off to the start they hoped after losing two games to perennial favorites in the AFC. The Colts lost two high scoring affairs to the Baltimore Ravens and Kansas City Chiefs and are looking to right the ship against the Houston Texan. FanDuel’s odds currently favor the Texans by 1.5 points. Those odds are much lower than Houston fans would have hoped for and are indicative of the poor start the Texans have put together on both sides of the ball. Jonathan Taylor powers the Colts’ offense with 190 yards through two games. I predict he will have another productive and efficient day given the Texans difficulties stopping the run. No Henry To’oTo’o or Kayden McDonald means the Texans are vulnerable up the middle of the defense. QB Daniel Jones has been thoroughly mediocre in his return from Achilles injury suffered last season. He has thrown two touchdowns and two interceptions. He has struggled to sustain drives and has not looked efficient in the red zone. Newly minted $114M man Alec Pierce has landed on Injured Reserve. He crushed the Texans last year and racked up 210 yards and three touchdowns in two games. His absence will be an immense blessing for a Texans defense surely in need of a reprieve and get-right game. As for the Texans’ offense, they quickly shifted away from the run against the Bengals, opting to throw the ball a career high 55 times for C.J. Stroud. This was ineffective and certainly not the game script from Offensive Coordinator Nick Caley. Expect Houston to commit, heavily to the run game and incorporate the screen game to break up the issues they’ve faced on offense. PREDICTION: Colts 24, Texans 17 The Texans offense have yet to put it together. Without WR Nico Collins in the line up there is no indication of their ability to score points. Plus, the Texans’ defense has been unusually porous to start the 2026 season, not to mention unable to convert any turnovers. Houston has to find a way to get WR Kayshon Boutte incorporated into the offense. Boutte leads the league in go-routes, but that’s simply not enough for him to positively impact this offense. Slants and screens are two easy options for the wide receiver to take more ownership of the air attack and help move the ball down the field. What separates these two teams is the Colts’ run game. Jonathan Taylor is the most effective weapon for either offense and will allow the Colts to control the tempo. Houston has yet to counter a strong rushing attack. QB Daniel Jones is fairly immobile, which is ideal for the Texans pass rush. In Week One, Bills QB Josh Allen detonated the Texans pass rush duo with his scrambling ability. Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter won’t have to worry about that with Jones, who has already been sacked twice this season. I predict Tyler Warren to have a very productive game against the Texans defense. He leads their team with nine receptions, but only 39 yards. Houston gave up play after play to Buffalo’s tight end Dalton Kincaid. Expect Jones to find Warren early and often on play action plays to decrease the pressure on the run game. The Colts late addition of Keenan Allen has paid dividends as his seven receptions is third on the team behind Josh Downs and Tyler Warren. He is facing a potential three-game suspension due to driving over the legal limit in Indianapolis earlier this month. If he plays he should be the focal point of CB Kamari Lassiter, who is desperately in need of a good game. The Texans have not let Lassiter and Derek Stingley Jr. follow specific receivers, which has led to ill-advised mismatches in the secondary. The Colts game presents an opportunity for Stingley Jr. to follow the faster Downs and Lassiter to pursue Allen. One player on the Texans offense to watch for is Jaylin Noel. He was featured more often this game than in previous contests, mostly out of desperation, but it’s a good sign of his growth and incorporation in Houston’s plans. Fans saw Dalton Schultz shine in a big role last week, which should most certainly be the case again if Nico Collins is sidelined with a hamstring injury again. Going 0-3 again is not ideal. The criticism and disgruntled emotions will be at an all-time high under the Ryans era. This team was supposed to be better than the last across the board and haven’t shown any progression on any of the fronts they addressed this offseason. The offensive line can’t pass protect or move the ball. The run game is putrid. Whoever plays safety next to Calen Bullock forgets how to play football (C.J. Gardner Johnson, Reed Blankenship). Will it be different this game and can the Texans right the ship earlier than last year? We’ll find out on Sunday.
author: Kenneth Levy

title: Five Good Texans Questions with Stampede Blue
summary: You stay in this game long enough and you start building relationships along the way. Chris Sheperd of Stampede Blue and I have been doing five questions for the last five years and it has been an enjoyable ride. Even though the Colts and Tecans are enemies on the field doesn’t mean we have to […]
full_text: You stay in this game long enough and you start building relationships along the way. Chris Sheperd of Stampede Blue and I have been doing five questions for the last five years and it has been an enjoyable ride. Even though the Colts and Tecans are enemies on the field doesn’t mean we have to be enemies in the proverbial press box. Yet again, the Texans and Colts stand in each other’s way for playoff contention. Two 0-2 teams are coming off of two tough weeks and that is where our conversation began. Battle Red Blog: Like the Texans, the Colts have started 0-2 but against quality opponents. Are you concerned or feel like the start is a function of the difficult competition? Chris Shepard: Most Colts fans believe the sky is falling and given the history of the last decade they may be right to believe that. I am less concerned than most but concerned all the same. The defense went through a big turnover this offseason. Colts fans were largely over linebacker Zaire Franklin on and off of the field, but he was a long tenured leader of the defense as was corner Kenny Moore. Indy was right to move on from them in an attempt to do a soft reset on a leadership group that had yet to find sustained success. Just because it was the right thing to do doesn’t mean it’s going to yield immediate positive results. The Colts added a lot of young players and lower level free agents and so far we’ve seen them struggle to get to speed. Week two was a large improvement for the defense but I expect this defense won’t hit it’s stride until week 8 or 9, if they ever come together at all. Facing Lamar Jackson and Patrick Mahomes back to back against a young defense with so many new pieces was always going to be difficult and while I don’t think CJ Stroud is in that tier of quarterbacks, it’s not like things are going to be significantly easier for them in week three. BRB: Injuries are a part of the game obviously. We all saw Alec Pierce leave the game on Sunday night. Are there any other injuries you are concerned about? CS: Sauce Gardner went out in the second half with an injury, he was able to return but he was in obvious pain. Sauce has been very good through two weeks so I’ll be monitoring his progress throughout the week. BRB: Who are some new faces we haven’t seen in this matchup that will play a key role on Sunday? CS: Rookie safety AJ Halucy has gotten every opportunity to contribute so far thus season. Halucy, a third round pick out of LSU, hasn’t been bad but he has made some rookie mistakes. I suspect they’ll continue to give him the majority of the snaps at strong safety and there is plenty of reason to believe he’ll make more of an impact as the season goes on. Rookie linebackers Bryce Boettcher (Oregon) and CJ Allen (Georgia) have been working their way into a linebacker rotation. Allen missed more than a month of training camp due to injury and is working his way back. Neither player has made much of an impact yet but week by week they should see more time on the field and week three should see another uptick of snaps for both. BRB: This is an annual question. Who are you most concerned about in the AFC South and how do you see the division shaking out? Which divisional opponent do Colts fans enjoy beating the most? CS: The Jaguars are my biggest concern followed closely by the Texans. Houston figured things out last season and while defensive success is more difficult to sustain year over year, DeMeco Ryans is a very good coach and I expect they’ll turn things around in short order. The Jaguars combination of Trevor Lawrence and Liam Coen has been solid. I’m less sold on Coen long term than I am on Ryans, I think that when things start to go bad for him he’s more likely to be unable to right the Jacksonville ship. But until that happens, the combo of Coen and Lawrence with that offense puts them at the top of the division. Ultimately, I think it’ll land on the Jaguars at the top and I hope Indy and Houston are in a battle for a wildcard spot headed into week 18 but given Houston’s recent history they absolutely have the advantage right now. BRB: Fanduel has the Texans favored by 2.5. How do you see the game going on Sunday? Are there any other bets you feel comfortable recommending? CS: I think that’s a fair line.Both teams are desperate and both are capable of winning. I see this one coming down to the wire, with both teams trading shots until the final moments. In games like this one anything can happen and while I hope the Colts pull it off, Houston being the favorite makes sense. We want to thank Chris for taking the time to answer our questions and for being such a joy to work with for all of these years. Remember, if you want to catch the best Colts coverage, please feel free to catch his site at Stampede Blue . We want to wish Chris the Colts the best of luck for the rest of the season. That is of course except for when they are playing the Texans.

title: 5 Questions with Battle Red Blog: will either team win?
summary: In Week 3 of 2026 our Indianapolis Colts will host the Houston Texans. Knowing the party was coming to town I sat down with Scott Barzilla of Battle Red Blog, SB Nation’s Houston Texans blog. We swapped questions and answers about both the Texans and the Colts and what follows is what I’ve learned about […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 20: Head coach DeMeco Ryans of the Houston Texans reacts after a touchdown by the Las Vegas Raiders in the fourth quarter during a preseason game at Reliant Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images In Week 3 of 2026 our Indianapolis Colts will host the Houston Texans . Knowing the party was coming to town I sat down with Scott Barzilla of Battle Red Blog , SB Nation’s Houston Texans blog. We swapped questions and answers about both the Texans and the Colts and what follows is what I’ve learned about this week’s enemy. You can find my answers to his questions here. Chris Shepherd: Based on the first two weeks of the season, if you were an offensive coordinator tasked with creating a game plan to attack the Texans defense, what does your plan look like? What areas of the field are you attacking, what weaknesses are you targeting? How do you beat this Texans defense? Scott Barzilla: I think you attack the interior of their defense with Jonathan Taylor. The edges are the strength of their defense and it keeps you ahead of the chains. If you get behind the sticks it’s going to be a long day. Chris Shepherd: From weeks one to two we saw a big improvement from the Indy defense. Granted that improvement went from lockout replacement players level to simply very bad NFL defense level, in what ways could the Colts defense prevent the Texans offense from righting the ship after a disappointing outing last week? Scott Barzilla: You stop the running game and make the Texans one dimensional. If Stroud has to win he won’t have Nico Collins to bail him out. You can pressure him and create some turnovers. Chris Shepherd: Through two games CJ Stroud is averaging nearly 314 passing yards per game but is only completing 60.2% of his passes, he has also only thrown for 2 touchdowns. What exactly has been the biggest problem with an offense that seems to be passing the ball so well? Scott Barzilla: The Texans have been playing from behind so they have been pass happy. The problem has been a lack of the running game and break downs in communication. Stroud had five drops last week which killed his percentage. Otherwise he’d be having a great season.. Chris Shepherd: Can you give me one player on offense and one on defense that Colts fans might not be familiar with who you expect to have an impact on Sunday night? Scott Barzilla: On defense I’d say we are due for some turnovers so I’d say Calen Bullock or Jalen Pitre could be the guys there. On offense I’d look for Marlin Klein to get a key catch or two with the receiving core undermanned. Chris Shepherd: How do you predict this game will play out? What does each team do well, where will they struggle and what’s the final score? Scott Barzilla: The Texans have won five in a row in this matchup and I’d expect a sixth. It will be a close game but I think a key turnover will make the difference late. Taylor worries me on the defensive end but nothing the Colts defense does scares me that much. And with that, ladies and gentlemen, our week three preview with the enemy is in the books. As always I want to thank Scott for working with me and giving us a a look into what the Houston Texans will bring to Indianapolis this weekend. Here’s to an injury free game. As always, go Colts.

title: Can Colts strike the win column to avoid 0-3 start?
summary: The Indianapolis Colts will trade their traditional look and debut their Anvil Strike Rivalries uniform, which is set to make its on-field appearance in Sunday’s home game against the AFC South foe Houston Texans.  Given that it’s the 50th meeting between the divisional rivals, the timing couldn’t be more fitting. The stampede will take the field […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 17: Indianapolis Head Coach Shane Steichen talks with Houston Texans Head Coach DeMeco Ryans prior to an NFL football game at NRG Stadium on September 17, 2023 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts will trade their traditional look and debut their Anvil Strike Rivalries uniform, which is set to make its on-field appearance in Sunday’s home game against the AFC South foe Houston Texans. Given that it’s the 50th meeting between the divisional rivals, the timing couldn’t be more fitting. The stampede will take the field sporting a metallic candy-blue helmet, designed specifically for the uniform. The darker jersey features a heather-gray, anthracite color scheme inspired by the heavier anvil steel. Sunday’s fit. 🔥 pic.twitter.com/KDkjXEzBRD — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) September 25, 2026 The horseshoe will still be there in the middle of the field to separate opposing territories, but it will be the first time in franchise history that has the horseshoe is integrated into the jersey design. The alternate Anvil Strike uniform is part of the NFL’s new rivalry series, a league-wide collaboration with Nike in an effort to celebrate the traditions, history and competitive spirit of divisional football. Colts owner and Chief Brand Officer Kalen Jackson mentioned on The Colts Show with JJ Stankevitz that the collaboration with Nike took more than two years to complete. Timeline check. pic.twitter.com/oIogve1PrR — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) September 24, 2026 Sunday’s matchup comes at a time when the Colts could desperately use a different look. It’s been past time to switch things up as Indianapolis has lost its last nine games, including the last four at home. The Colts last home victory was 11 months ago against the Tennessee Titans. The Colts own a 33-15-1 all-time record against the Texans. Indy dominated the early years of the series, winning 15 of the first 16 meetings during Peyton Manning’s prime. DeMeco Ryans’ Texans have controlled the rivalry recently, winning each of the last five meetings during the Shane Steichen era. Despite the winless record, all five games were decided by one possession and the average margin of victory has been just 4.2 points. Both head coaches were first-time hires by their respective clubs in 2023. Ryans was named the Pro Football Writer’s Association Coach of the Year in his debut campaign and currently holds a 32-21 regular season record with a 3-3 playoff record in Houston. The biggest disparity between the divisional foes is on the defensive side of the football. The Colts have struggled on the dark side and rank dead last in total defense, allowing an eye-popping 515 yards per game. The secondary has surrendered 338 passing yards per game, also last in the league. The Colts have allowed 74 points and carry a minus-225 yardage differential through the first two weeks, which are all dead last in the rankings. After a gut-wrenching, 33-30 overtime road loss to the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday Night Football, Indianapolis enters must-win territory to avoid the dreaded 0-3 start. Only seven NFL teams have recovered from a 0-3 start, although the Texans are the lone team to accomplish that feat this century in 2018 and 2025. Now Houston flies into Indy, aiming to avoid another 0-3 start. The Colts host the Texans on Sunday inside Lucas Oil Stadium, with kickoff set for 1 p.m.

title: Colts just proved why the NFL stands for the “No Fun League”
summary: The NFL loves money. They do anything and everything to get as much of it as possible. Stream the season on 29 different platforms? No problem. Span the globe and play in 10 different countries? You bet. They love it so much that they are willing to fine players like Indianapolis Colts’ Matt Goncalves $9K […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - SEPTEMBER 20: Tyler Warren #84 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates a touchdown with Matt Goncalves #71 in the first quarter of an NFL game between the Indianapolis Colts and Kansas City Chiefs on Sep 20, 2026 at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The NFL loves money. They do anything and everything to get as much of it as possible. Stream the season on 29 different platforms? No problem. Span the globe and play in 10 different countries? You bet. They love it so much that they are willing to fine players like Indianapolis Colts’ Matt Goncalves $9K for his celebration against the Chiefs. It’s a matter that is out of hand. What was Goncalves’ offense? Surely he must have gestured towards the other team in a crude manner, or maybe he inappropriately engaged fans on the sideline. Nope. After receiving the ball on a Tyler Warren touchdown, Goncalves acted like he was taking a drink. It was labeled as an “offensive demonstration”. More: Colts guard Matt Goncalves also was fined $8,847 for engaging Sunday night in what the NFL called an offensive demonstration. “Your imitation of chugging a beer constituted an offensive demonstration…in poor taste.” After Tyler Warren scored, he gave the football to… pic.twitter.com/7y50i79uXt — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) September 24, 2026 Mind you, this is the same league that promotes adult beverages every five seconds on their commercial breaks. The same league that has official tailgate and pregame areas sponsored by these brands. A league that sells a copious amount in the stadium and has designated areas in the stadium named after these companies has the gall to call this offensive. If the ad running on your television during an NFL game isn’t for an adult beverage, it’s for a betting site. If the ad isn’t for a betting site, it’s for an adult beverage. Taunting and lewd gestures towards other players and fans are acceptable as fineable offenses. Heck, even fining players $9K like the league did Goncalves is ok too, if the NFL is willing to uproot its current business model. This type of culture has permeated the NFL so much that I wouldn’t have been surprised to see that celebration officially sponsored by one of these companies. That’s how often fans are hit with it. The “No Fun League” strikes again. Young, impressionable children can’t see that type of celebration on television while their parent is building a can tower next to them on the table during the broadcast. They are blasted on repeat by ads and in person sponsorships, but when a player chugs a drink, which could have been literally anything, that is a step too far. Give me a break.

full_text: Cleveland Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson (4) runs past Jacksonville Jaguars defensive end Arik Armstead (91) during the fourth quarter of an NFL football matchup Sunday, Sept. 15, 2024 at EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville, Fla. title: Jaguars vs. Patriots predictions: Brenton Strange is due
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars (1-1) are back at EverBank Stadium to face the New England Patriots (1-1) in Week 3. The teams last met in Week 7 of the 2024 season, when Tank Bigsby rushed for a career-high 118 yards and 2 touchdowns in a 34-16 Jags win at Wembley Stadium. According to FanDuel Sportsbook, the Jaguars […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - SEPTEMBER 20: Tight end Brenton Strange (85) of the Jacksonville Jaguars pulls in a reception from quarterback Trevor Lawrence (16) during the first half a game against the Denver Broncos on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026, at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, Colo. (Photo by Timothy Hurst/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images) | Denver Post via Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars (1-1) are back at EverBank Stadium to face the New England Patriots (1-1) in Week 3. The teams last met in Week 7 of the 2024 season, when Tank Bigsby rushed for a career-high 118 yards and 2 touchdowns in a 34-16 Jags win at Wembley Stadium. According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Jaguars are 2.5-point favorites against the Patriots this week. Home-field advantage is generally worth a 3-point swing, so on a neutral field, Jacksonville would be 0.5-point underdogs. I have a feeling that’s the mentality the team will be operating with anyway after last week’s narrow loss at Mile High. Let’s get to some predictions. Prediction #1 Did you know that the Jaguars were 11-1 last season when Brenton Strange played? He was a pillar of Liam Coen’s offense, and Jacksonville secured him on a long-term extension in the offseason. Though two games this year, Strange only has 4 catches (5 targets) for 40 yards and 1 touchdown. Total. There may be “a lot of mouths to feed” between Parker Washington and Brian Thomas Jr. and Jakobi Meyers in the wide receiver room, but Trevor Lawrence already has 52 pass attempts. That equates to a 9.6% target share for Strange so far. When healthy last season, he had a 16% target share. Good news: this underwhelming box-score start is nothing to fret about. Strange is due for work in the passing game, and not just because of natural regression after a small sample of games. He ran crisp routes against the Broncos in Week 2, but for various reasons, Lawrence wasn’t looking his way a few times when he popped wide open. I think the team could see that on tape and say, “Oh, yeah. We just paid this guy because we think he’s really good. Maybe we should try to get him the ball more often.” If/when New England’s interior pass rush disrupts Lawrence on Sunday, it’ll be even more of a reason to lean into short-area passing concepts featuring Strange. The prediction: Brenton Strange matches his current 2026 receiving stats Strange has +300 odds on FanDuel to score a touchdown, and his receiving yardage over/under line is set at 27.5 yards. Prediction #2 Jacksonville’s run defense has merely been above average this season after being the league’s best in 2025. The fact that the Broncos ran free for 1st downs to clinch last week’s game was alarming, to say the least. Expect the Jaguars to tighten up against a Patriots offense that wants to run the ball but isn’t all that threatening when it does. While Rhamondre Stevenson is among the most underappreciated rushers in football, he’s a jack-of-all-trades with no elite traits and a real issue holding onto the rock. And while 2025 second-round pick TreVeyon Henderson is among the most explosive rushers in football, he requires a wide-open rushing lane to inflict maximum damage. How valuable is a slugger if he can only connect on fastballs down the middle? New England’s running back room is solid yet unremarkable. Their starting offensive line looked promising to start the season, but right guard Mike Onwenu fractured his ankle in Week 2. Jacksonville ought to shut down the opposing running game, the same way they did so many times last season, but the real question is whether they can contain a dual-threat quarterback. Can the Jags prevent out-of-structure playmaking from last year’s MVP runner-up? The prediction: Drake Maye leads the Patriots in rushing yards On FanDuel, Maye’s rushing yards over/under line is set at 26.5 yards. Stevenson’s line is at 37.5 yards; Henderson’s line is at 41.5 yards. Prediction #3 Josh Hines-Allen has played 112 NFL games (including playoffs). Last week’s loss in Denver was just his seventh career game without recording a pressure. According to NFL Pro, Hines-Allen has a career-low 9.3% so far this season. He recorded a double-digit pressure rate in each of his seven prior seasons. Jacksonville’s pass rush was already a concern going into this season, mostly because of the apparent lack of depth behind Hines-Allen and Travon Walker. If Hines-Allen isn’t playing like a No. 1 guy, the Jags could be screwed! Fortunately, like Strange, I expect Hines-Allen to bounce back. It feels like we do this every season — he goes through a dry spell, then fans scapegoat him for a holistic roster issue, then he eventually re-finds his dominance. After posting a Tony Snell stat line against All-Pro left tackle Garrett Bowles, Hines-Allen has a great opportunity to turn his season around on Sunday against Will Campbell. The Patriots’ 2025 first-round pick probably isn’t as bad as he’s publicly perceived after a rocky rookie postseason — and his stats this year are actually pretty solid — but at the end of the day, Campbell should have trouble handling Hines-Allen one-on-one. The former has T-Rex arms and a poor anchor. The latter tends to feast against inferior competition. Remember those “ Have a Day! ” social media graphics the NFL used to post? If they were still doing that, I’d bet Hines-Allen would have one after playing the Patriots. The prediction: Josh Hines-Allen records a sack, a tipped pass, and a turnover Let us know your Week 3 predictions in the comments below! DUUUVAL! Join the game-day conversation on the SB Nation app!
