title: Jets vs Lions: Five Questions with Pride of Detroit
summary: The New York Jets are on the road on Sunday for the 3rd game of their 2026 campaign. They will be facing the Detroit Lions. The Lions are 1-1 on the year. They are coming off a rough 41 -31 loss to the Buffalo Bills last week after squeaking by the New Orleans Saints 31 […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Jahmyr Gibbs #0 of the Detroit Lions celebrates with Amon-Ra St. Brown #14 after scoring a touchdown against the Buffalo Bills during the second quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New York Jets are on the road on Sunday for the 3rd game of their 2026 campaign. They will be facing the Detroit Lions. The Lions are 1-1 on the year. They are coming off a rough 41 -31 loss to the Buffalo Bills last week after squeaking by the New Orleans Saints 31 – 30 the week before. Previewing this matchup, Ryan Mathews, Senior Editor at Pride of Detroit , was kind enough to answer a few questions regarding the 2026 Detroit Lions. 1. The Lions have had all kinds of problems on defense so far, ranking 31st in the NFL in both yards allowed and points allowed. Is that just a product of who they’ve faced, or are there deeper underlying problems here? What have been the main issues so far? There’s certainly something to be said about the quality of opponents they faced in the first two weeks. Buffalo’s offense ranks first in EPA/play this season, and New Orleans had the 11th ranked offense in that same statistic last week against Baltimore. But it would be a bald-faced lie to suggest the Lions defense simply found themselves up against two great offenses and there’s not much they could have done to prevent what happened. The Lions defense looked stout in the first half against the Saints in Week 1, but ever since then, they’ve been taken to task: Detroit has allowed points on 11 of their last 14 drives, 10 of them going for touchdowns. The underlying problem has been missed assignments and miscommunication plaguing the backend of their defense. Detroit’s secondary is at the center of their issues, but the defense has dramatically underperformed in just about every aspect: defensive penalties to keep drives alive, not getting off the field on third down, allowing bad plays to snowball and lead to further miscues and mistakes. It’s been a nightmare, and a lot of the attention has turned toward Kelvin Sheppard, Detroit’s defensive coordinator who took over last season for Aaron Glenn. Some theories suggest Sheppard needs to simplify things a bit, let his players play without overloading them mentally which seems to be leading to some of these breakdowns in coverage. Time is ticking for the Lions to get these things cleaned up sooner rather than later when the offense is, for the most part, pulling their weight, putting up 31 points in back-to-back weeks. 2. The Lions looked like Super Bowl contenders two years ago before having an off year last year. Of course these things are relative, as a 9-8 season would be a minor miracle for the Jets, but for the Lions it was an off year. Are you expecting a big bounce back year this year? If so, what are the factors which should make a difference to the upside, and if not, why not? Detroit’s season last year was the first true misstep of the Dan Campbell era. It felt like the first time the team failed to meet preseason expectations. Entering the 2026 season, the expectations are clearly marked as not only a return to the playoffs, but playoff success–something that escaped Detroit in 2024 when the injuries on defense were just too much to overcome. Those are more than fair expectations for a football team with as much top-end talent as this roster holds. From the look of things to start the season, it’s going to be on the defensive side of the ball to reach their goals. From the coaching staff to the players, they’re going to need to coalesce and find some more consistent play, not putting the brunt of the load on the offense to constantly bail them out. 3. Could you give us a synopsis of what the 2026 Lions draft class has looked like so far, and what you expect from them as the year goes on? We’ve only seen one week of real, regular season football from Blake Miller, the Lions’ first-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft. Early returns have been very promising, he didn’t look out of place against the Saints in Week 1, but after suffering a knee injury and Detroit having a quick turnaround for “Thursday Night Football” against the Bills, the Lions opted to keep him on the sideline so he’d be ready for Week 3. Reports suggested he could have played last week had Detroit been afforded a full week of practice, so his health seems to be trending in the right direction–and it seems like the Lions are going to need him for this matchup with David Bailey. As for the rest of this class, second-round pick Derrick Moore, an edge defender from Michigan, missed some time in the preseason with a groin injury, but had really impressed in training camp. He’s been on a bit of a pitch count as Detroit has folded him into the defense, playing limited snaps through the first two weeks of his NFL career–18 against the Saints in Week 1 and 17 the following week against the Bills. He’s got a strong bull rush and plays the run well, a staple amongst Lions’ defensive ends, so it’ll be interesting to see if he sees the field a bit more this week. Linebacker Jimmy Rolder has been a healthy inactive so far through two weeks, Keith Abney was forced into play when injuries happened in Week 1, but he was a healthy inactive last week. One player who has played a lot is Skyler Gill-Howard, a sixth-round pick and former teammate of David Bailey at Texas Tech. He’s primarily a pass-rusher at this point in his development, effective in getting skinny and knifing through the offensive linemen along the interior. He’s played a healthy dose of snaps so far, more than expected, for sure. 4. Every team has a player or two who may be somewhat unfamiliar to other teams’ fans but is known to be an unsung hero by fans of his own team. Who are the Lions’ unsung heroes? If possible give us one guy on each side of the ball. Full transparency, there’s only one player who comes to mind: Derrick Barnes. The veteran linebacker is in a contract season and he’s been one of the best players on Detroit’s defense through two weeks. He’s the team’s SAM linebacker, so he wears a lot of hats for this defense. He’s an edge setter, a pass rusher, a coverage guy; he does it all at the second level for Detroit. Barnes has an interception and a couple of sacks on the season so far, and he’s playing a ton in comparison to past seasons. 5. If you were an opposing head coach, how would you attack this Lions team on offense and on defense? If I’m Aaron Glenn, I’m going to test this Lions’ secondary early and often. Despite Geno Smith being a turnover-prone quarterback, it’s not going to hurt the Jets to try and push the ball downfield with the likes of Garrett Wilson and Kenyon Sadiq lining up for New York. The key for the Jets in this one is to try and get ahead on the scoreboard early. If the Jets can dictate the game script, it can force the Lions to play outside of themselves by throwing the ball more than they’d like to. In turn, that would give New York’s pass rush a chance to force negative plays and turnovers. It will be key for the Jets to slow down Jahmyr Gibbs and the Lions running game, force them into third-and-long situations, and make Detroit feel as uncomfortable as possible in their own home. Jared Goff is at his best when he’s attacking the middle of the field, and while it’s easier said than done, if the Jets can get pressure with four and muddy the area in between the hash marks, it will give New York their best chance at shutting down this potent Lions’ attack on offense.

title: Eagles opposing player to stop, Week 3 edition
summary: The Bears’ Ben Johnson and the Eagles’ Nick Sirianni may be the two most annoying head coaches in the NFL today. They are also among the best. But this is where Johnson is one over on Sirianni. During Black Friday last November, very audible “Let’s go Bears” chants echoed inside the walls from a three-quarters […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - NOVEMBER 28: Kyle Monangai #25 of the Chicago Bears celebrates after scoring a 4 yard touchdown against the Philadelphia Eagles during the fourth quarter in the game at Lincoln Financial Field on November 28, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Bears’ Ben Johnson and the Eagles’ Nick Sirianni may be the two most annoying head coaches in the NFL today. They are also among the best. But this is where Johnson is one over on Sirianni. During Black Friday last November, very audible “Let’s go Bears” chants echoed inside the walls from a three-quarters empty Lincoln Financial Field in the last three minutes of Chicago’s 24-15 victory, which was nowhere near as indicative of how lopsided that debacle was. Chicago outgained the Eagles by almost 200 yards on the ground, giving up a season-high 281 yards rushing to the Eagles’ 87. The Bears ran off 85 plays to the Eagles’ 51, and almost doubled the Eagles in time of possession, 39:18 to 20:42. Everyone on and off field found out who Kyle Monangai was, after he rushed for 130 yards. The Bears did not need star quarterback Caleb Williams then and will not have him Monday night when the Eagles seek their revenge for last year’s embarrassment. Williams is likely out with a hamstring injury, backup Tyson Bagent is in concussion protocol and probably will not play either, leaving the Bears with 38-year-old fossil Case Keenum. Keenum, or no Keenum, he may be nothing more than handing the ball off to Monangai and former St. Joe’s Prep star and former Eagle D’Andre Swift. Those two will be helped by Bears’ right guard Jonah Jackson, another Bear with more Philadelphia ties, as a former star at Rutgers and Penncrest High School in Media, Delaware County, Pennsylvania, just outside Philadelphia. Chicago has the No. 1 rushing offense in the NFL, averaging 212.5 yards rushing a game, along with an NFL-best 6.1 yards rushing per carry, and NFL-high 35 rushes a game. The Eagles will try and stop that attack with a rushing defense that is giving up 127.0 yards rushing per game, ranked 24th in the NFL. This is also an Eagles’ team that yielded an embarrassing 27-yard run—on a third-and-22 play—to Tyjae Spears. Jalyx Hunt, who has been somewhat disappointing at the edge, lost outside contain, tackle Moro Ojomo got thrown down, three plays after making a tackle for loss, and safety Marcus Epps took a bad angle as Spears went by him down the left sideline. If it were Monangai, the play may have wound up in the end zone. Eagles’ defensive Vic Fangio remembers last year’s Black Friday game and the struggles the Eagles’ defense had against the Bears’ running game. “We’ve got to play it better, obviously,” Fangio said. “They are one of the better running teams in the league. They’ve got a really great O-line, great backs. Their scheme is good. We’re going to have to play it a whole lot better.” The Bears have scored 10 TDs this season—eight have come rushing the ball. With Williams being out, that diminishes much of the Bears’ running threat. Johnson and his staff performed a masterclass of strategy in totally outcoaching Sirianni the last time these teams met. Johnson is very capable of out scheming Sirianni and Fangio again. The Eagles should win this game, though becoming heavily reliant on one player—Jalen Hurts—to continue bailing them out behind a porous offensive line tends to have a short shelf life of success, and can finish your quarterback for the season. How long can Hurts stay upright and healthy behind this mess? Maybe that gets answered Monday night.

Caleb Williams has a hamstring injury, Tyson Bagent is in concussion protocol, so Case Keenum took the first-team practice reps on Wednesday. I’m going to assume Keenum is starting, so I won’t talk much about quarterback in this one. The Bears ran for 281 yards against the Eagles last November, and Ben Johnson has built another offense that can make life very difficult if the run game gets going. Fangio and his defense will remember that afternoon. Pass Game Williams is special. He’s not consistently good, but his highs are special. I know that is hardly a groundbreaking statement, but it matters when evaluating the Bears because he can make a well-defended play look badly defended in about two seconds. He is outstanding on the move, keeps looking downfield while escaping pressure and has the arm to find a receiver long after the original concept should have ended. The Panthers game showed the frightening version of this offense. The Vikings game showed the other side. Flores was causing problems before Williams got hurt. Minnesota constantly threatened pressure, disrupted the timing of the passing game, and forced the Bears into uncomfortable downs. Williams can evade a free rusher better than almost anyone, but that does not mean the offense can live indefinitely with defenders arriving before its intermediate routes develop. If he plays on Monday, the hamstring also raises an obvious question about how freely he can escape. If he does not, the Eagles are facing a fundamentally different kind of quarterback. Ben Johnson has said he does not anticipate dramatically changing the game plan based on the starter. I believe him in terms of the structure of the offense, but no coach can replace Williams’ movement and creativity. Keenum is experienced and should be able to run the system, but the Eagles will be much less concerned about him turning a broken play into a 25-yard gain. Bagent is more willing to take chances and push the ball if he clears protocol, although that can create opportunities for the defense too. What surprised me while watching the first two games was how straightforward the Bears’ starting point has been. I expected more of the varied, puller-heavy run game associated with Johnson’s time in Detroit and perhaps more constant motion. Instead, the Bears have repeatedly lined up under center, run outside zone, and built passes from that same presentation. The lack of variety in the core run concept should not be confused with a lack of imagination. Johnson changes the formations, personnel, and accompanying routes so that the defense keeps seeing familiar movement with a different answer attached. One of my favorite examples has a receiver moving through the C-gap. It looks like the sort of insert action that could bring an extra blocker into the run fit. Instead, the receiver continues upfield and becomes part of a three-level stretch in the passing game. A defender trained by the previous runs to react to movement through that gap now has to decide whether to fit the run, pick up the route, or pass it to someone else. Johnson makes you cover every blade of grass, and he is particularly good at creating that moment of indecision. 3) No surprise, but they marry the run and pass game together very well. That's why they love running from under center. This is one of the coolest plays I've seen this season. Like the Rams, they frequently use a C-gap insert blocker in the run game. This time, they use a WR… pic.twitter.com/RlzUNwRjO1 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 24, 2026 This Cole Kmet leak is beautiful, too. The Bears show outside zone to the left while bringing a tight end across the formation to block back the other way. They use that movement in their actual running game, which is why the fake is convincing. This time, Cole Kmet slips out into space. It is easy to describe as a play-action pass; the impressive part is how closely the pass resembles a run the defense has already had to respect. One false step from a linebacker or safety is enough. This is Ben Johnson’s secret. The run and pass game are as well connected as anyone’s offense. 4) This is as good as it gets. They fake outside zone to the left after using this motion with the TE coming across the formation and blocking back the other way (which they do a lot in the run game) and they have Cole Kmet on the TE leak route. It's beautiful design and… pic.twitter.com/9UVcLcOSJ2 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 24, 2026 The receiving group gives Johnson several ways to finish those designs. Rome Odunze can win downfield, and Luther Burden III can turn a quick completion into more. Kmet and Colston Loveland threaten the middle of the field, which is exactly where a defense can become vulnerable if its second-level defenders are responding to outside zone. Kalif Raymond has been heavily involved, which is a little surprising, given he hasn’t had much success. The Bears also want more than quick throws. Their intermediate routes often develop quite deep, and they will send receivers vertically to create space underneath and across the field. I would be wary of playing passively and assuming a backup quarterback cannot hurt the Eagles. Give Johnson enough time, and he will find a way to get somebody open. Conversely, if the Eagles can make the quarterback throw before the deeper over or vertical route develops, the offense becomes far less threatening. That was a significant part of the Vikings’ success. 7) It might be different this week without Caleb, but the Bears want to throw the ball down the field. I think if you play passively, Ben Johnson will find a way to get receivers open. Their intermediate routes are often deep, and if you can get after them with pressure, you can… pic.twitter.com/x6RPcGWKws — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 24, 2026 This brings us to protection, which I think is one of the most interesting parts of the matchup. The Bears’ line can move people in the running game. Darnell Wright is an outstanding right tackle, Joe Thuney and Jonah Jackson give them quality at guard, and they showed against the Panthers how well they can work together on zone runs. But I thought center Garrett Bradbury looked vulnerable when the Panthers and Vikings stressed him with stunts and twists. The Vikings, in particular, made the Bears communicate against changing pressure looks, and there were snaps where the protection never looked comfortable. Fangio is not Flores. I can’t imagine the Eagles spending the entire night showing six defenders at the line and sending pressure at Minnesota’s rate. I do think this is a good week to mix in stunts and simulated pressures, though. Make Bradbury identify the rush, make the line pass defenders off, and see whether a four-man rush can create a problem after the Bears have accounted for the wrong threats. That fits Fangio far better than asking him to abandon his normal approach and blitz constantly. 5) I do think that center Garrett Bradbury is a weakness right now with the Bears' line. The Vikings put pressure and succeeded, as did the Panthers on this rep. Fangio doesn't often send more than 4 rushers, but he might have to mix it up a bit this week. I'll be interested to… pic.twitter.com/JZpJ2mtnH0 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 24, 2026 The Eagles should also watch who the Bears leave in protection.…

full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: DeVonta Smith #6 of the Philadelphia Eagles walks through the tunnel against the Washington Commanders during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! To no surprise, Smitty is off to a strong start. Did anyone actually question if he could be WR1? That never shouldn’t been in doubt, if it even was at all. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … NFL wide receiver rankings: Jaxon Smith-Njigba leads top 32 – PFF DeVonta Smith, Philadelphia Eagles. Smith has benefited from the departure of A.J. Brown this offseason, averaging 2.30 yards per route run and ranking fourth at the position with a 91.4 PFF receiving grade. Now the No. 1 target in Philadelphia, he has a strong chance to put together the best season of his career. Eagles vs. Bears Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 3 enemy – BGN 4 – What’s the biggest matchup in the Bears’ favor and the biggest matchup against their favor? Well, I think the easiest one is the biggest disadvantage, and that will be the Eagles offensive line vs. the Bears defensive line. I understand Landon Dickerson is out, and the Eagles offensive line isn’t quite what it used to be, but it’s still a strong unit, and the Bears defensive line just isn’t. If the Philly OL can’t control the line of scrimmage, that would be rather surprising. I think the biggest advantage for them is the fact that the Eagles are struggling to stop the run right now, and the Bears block it extremely well. Maybe it’s a cliché, but I think this game is going to come down to controlling the line of scrimmage. Both teams have strong offensive lines and have a chance to control the line when they have the ball. I think the Bears need to really have long drives and keep their defense off the field. Can they do it without Caleb Williams? We will see on Monday night. Eagles mailbag: OL talk galore: Regrets? Trades? Reason for hope? – PhillyVoice Question from @jjapostolico (via Bluesky): Do Jurgens’ and Dickerson’s health make them less viable than the young guys like Drew Kendall and Willie Lampkin? Dickerson has been a great player for the last half decade for the Eagles. He was a first-round talent who they got in Round 2 because he had major injury concerns. I think that when they drafted him they knew he wasn’t going to have some sort of 12-year career, and they got a bunch of Pro Bowl seasons out of him. But it does feel like the end is near, and we could kind of see it in training camp, even before he performed poorly Week 1 against the Commanders. The younger guys are more viable options than him at this point. Jurgens has kind of gotten lumped in with Dickerson because he had injury issues all last season and both guys went to Colombia for stem cell treatments during the offseason. But to me, Jurgens looked fine in training camp, at least compared to Dickerson. In Week 1, Jurgens had a couple of penalties in the first quarter, but I thought he played well enough otherwise. Obviously, he had a terrible game Week 2 against Simmons after he was forced into a new role. But I’m not yet ready to say that he’s a candidate for replacement in the starting lineup. Week 3 NFL game preview: Chicago Bears vs. Philadelphia Eagles – Windy City Gridiron The first primetime game for the 2026 Chicago Bears has lost much of its luster since the team will most likely be starting its third quarterback on Monday night. The Bears welcome the Philadelphia Eagles to Soldier Field in what should have been a great matchup of historical franchises with young quarterbacks dueling it out. But the NFL is a fickle thing. Bears head coach Ben Johnson has to navigate his first game without his QB1 or QB2. And the Eagles, coming in 2-0 but not looking dominant, have a lot to prove. Beyond wanting to flush the memories of Black Friday last season, when the Bears completely dominated them. The Eagles want to make a statement that they’re back to being true contenders and that their new offense is working well. Even with a third QB, it should be an interesting game. Let’s get into the opponent then. One thing we’ve learned about the Eagles at every position group through two weeks: Offense edition – PHLY Eagles Tight end: Howie Roseman’s view of the position needs to evolve. I wonder, if given truth serum as he often likes to say, if the tight end position is the group Howie Roseman would most like a mulligan on from this offseason. For as much credit as Roseman should get for rebuilding the Eagles receiving corps in a post-A.J. Brown world, there are as many if not more questions about whether his additions at tight end are sufficient for the offense Mannion wants to run. At the start of the offseason, Roseman said he needed to change the way he viewed the position to better reflect the value of versatility on the perimeter rather than prioritizing capable pass-catching options, something that has accelerated league-wide even further this season. According to TruMedia, the Rams, Bills, Bears, and Ravens have all run more plays out of 13 personnel through two weeks than any team did this time last season. The Rams and Bills in particular have double the snaps with three tight ends on the field this year than last year’s leader (the Arizona Cardinals with 20 snaps). Watching these teams, it’s not hard to understand why they’ve shifted toward getting heavier personnel sets on the field. It often forces modern defenses set up to play with five defensive backs to instead play out of their base personnel groupings with one fewer and gives the offense an advantage on outside-zone runs in particular because of the improved blocking on the outside. And for teams like the Rams and Bills, the versatility of their tight-end rooms allows them to still throw out of those looks without sacrificing too much of a threat downfield. According to TruMedia, the Bills have generated four explosive plays out of 13-personnel this season, more than a handful of offenses have managed overall this season. At least through two weeks, the Eagles tight end room seems behind the curve. Eli Stowers projected as a receiving-only tight end even before a disappointing summer ended with a quad strain that landed him on injured reserve. Johnny Mundt’s addition gave them the option to put two trusted blocking options on the field to start the season, but Mundt’s even struggled at times in understandably difficult matchups with bigger defensive linemen. With Dallas Goedert sidelined and Zach Ertz stepping into his role, the room is not tailor-made for this outside zone-based system Mannion wants to run. It may be one of Roseman’s biggest misses this offseason, especially considering the questions about Stowers’ usage will likely extend beyond just his rookie season. (Michael Jordan) and, you know, build relationships with him and Tom Brady and all these other guys. Steve McNair is the only one that I’ve truly looked up to and watched and been enamored by and never got to meet him. So I think that was special for that reason. I was reminded of that when we pulled up to the stadium and it kind of hit me there.” The…

summary: The 1-1 Steelers take on the 2-0 Bengals this week as both teams open AFC North play. full_text: CINCINNATI, OHIO - OCTOBER 16: Pat Freiermuth #88 of the Pittsburgh Steelers runs the ball after a catch to score a 68 yard touchdown against the Cincinnati Bengals during the fourth quarter in the game at Paycor Stadium on October 16, 2025 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Photo by Michael Hickey/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 1-1 Steelers take on the 2-0 Bengals this week as both teams open AFC North play. Cincinnati, coming off a 20-6 win over the Texans last week, is on a different trajectory from the Steelers, who left Week 2 with a 20-6 loss to the Patriots. As a result, FanDuel Sportsbook has the Bengals as 3.5-point favorites heading into the weekend. Division games have a way of being unpredictable, especially this early in the season. That said, here are three predictions for Sunday’s matchup: Steelers Nation, bring the party to the SB Nation app! Connect with fellow fans and talk through every hard hit, huge play and dramatic finish. Chat live during the game Enjoy fewer ads Move seamlessly between communities Comment and post faster Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Pat Freiermuth has a big game The Bengals defense has struggled to contain tight ends to open the season, with Houston’s Dalton Schultz and Foster Moreau combining for 14 catches and 174 yards last week against Cincinnati. That’s a promising matchup for Steelers’ tight end Pat Freiermuth, who has averaged over 70 receiving yards in his last four games against the Bengals. And this year, Freiermuth has been a much bigger part of the Pittsburgh offense than in 2025; though two weeks this season, he’s already logged a team-best nine receptions. All signs point to another productive outing for Freiermuth on Sunday. The Steelers defense takes a step back While the Steelers’ defense hasn’t been without hiccups to start the season, it’s largely been one of the NFL’s best units, ranking top 10 in both yards and points allowed per game through two weeks. However, they haven’t faced an offense as strong as Cincinnati’s yet. In Week 1, the Steelers drew a favorable matchup against the Falcons with Cooper Rush at quarterback. And in Week 2, Pittsburgh performed solidly limiting Drake Maye and the Patriots, but New England was without its top receiver in A.J. Brown. This week, the Steelers won’t be facing a short-handed opponent. The Bengals feature quarterback Joe Burrow along with one of the league’s best wide receiver rooms in Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. Pittsburgh had some flaws in coverage and tackling last week, especially at the safety position, which will only be more tested against Cincinnati. Pittsburgh could really use Joey Porter Jr. this week, but even if he does play, it’ll be a difficult first assignment after being limited or a non-participant in practice since the summer. The Steelers have the league’s No. 3 passing defense through two weeks. Don’t expect the numbers to remain that elite against the Bengals. Jaylen Warren has more receiving than rushing yards With Rico Dowdle out against the Bengals, expect a heavy dose of Jaylen Warren at running back on Sunday. Warren himself is questionable, but seems likely to play. Steelers RBs coach Ramon Chinyoung on the RB rotation this week with Rico Dowdle likely being out: "With Rico being in the position he is now, Jaylen (Warren) is going to go out, he's going lead the group and when he needs a breather, we'll make sure he can receive that so he… — Nick Farabaugh (@FarabaughFB) September 25, 2026 That said, don’t expect a productive rushing game from Warren. The Steelers’ offensive line has struggled through two weeks and might shuffle its lineup ahead of Week 3. And the Bengals have the league’s third-strongest rushing defense through two weeks of the season, largely due to elite nose tackle Dexter Lawrence. As a result, the Steelers might lean into Warren’s yards after catch ability as a dump-off option in the passing game, especially with quarterback Aaron Rodgers getting rid of the ball quickly against an improved Bengals pass rush this year. Warren hasn’t had the most productive start to the season, with just 89 total rushing yards and 61 as a receiver through two games. Still, he’s the team’s third-leading pass catcher thus far, and is due for more involvement on offense this week. What are your predictions for Steelers vs. Bengals? Join the BTSC comment section and let us know!

title: Aaron Rodgers praises rookie offensive lineman’s development
summary: It’s only a matter of time before Max Iheanachor becomes the Pittsburgh Steelers’ starting right tackle. The only question is how fast the clock is moving. The Steelers have allowed 29 pressures and six sacks of Aaron Rodgers through two games and could look to make a change at any point. Pittsburgh’s offensive line hasn’t […]
full_text: It’s only a matter of time before Max Iheanachor becomes the Pittsburgh Steelers’ starting right tackle. The only question is how fast the clock is moving. The Steelers have allowed 29 pressures and six sacks of Aaron Rodgers through two games and could look to make a change at any point. Pittsburgh’s offensive line hasn’t made a good first impression under Mike McCarthy and James Campen as the Steelers are 30th in total offense (278.5 yards). As Rodgers’ career winds to an end this season and Iheanachor’s just begins, the future Hall of Fame quarterback sees good things ahead for the rookie tackle. “I think he’s got a really bright future,” Rodgers told the media Wednesday . “In one sense he’s raw because he hasn’t played football that long. The other sense, he’s got a beautiful set.” Rodgers is impressed by how Iheanachor considers himself and the technique that he’s developed. “You don’t say that about every tackle,” Rodgers said. “There’s nice sets, and then there’s beautiful sets.” Aaron Rodgers said when he’s ready, Max Iheanachor is going to be a staple of the #Steelers offensive line for a long time. Compared him to a couple of the best tackles he’s played with in terms of his set pic.twitter.com/kJozfmYJep — 93.7 The Fan (@937theFan) September 23, 2026 The Steelers selected Iheanachor with the 21st pick in the 2026 NFL Draft after only playing football for five years. Iheanachor didn’t play high school football and began his journey in community college before transferring to Arizona State in 2023. He was the sixth tackle taken in the draft and the last of a strong class, before a sizable dip in potential that the Steelers didn’t want to miss out on. If the Steelers are going to make a run at the AFC North and make the playoffs in back-to-back years, the offensive line needs to keep Rodgers upright and create time. Rodgers only missed one game last season, but has already taken multiple big hits that would leave any 42-year-old in significant pain.

full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - SEPTEMBER 20: Aaron Rodgers #8 of the Pittsburgh Steelers fumbles the ball against Christian Barmore #90 of the New England Patriots during the fourth quarter of the game at Gillette Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Winslow Townson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers were outclassed by the New England Patriots on Sunday, 20-3. Pittsburgh’s offense looked sluggish and struggled to move the ball very much at all against a stout Patriots defense. Despite another strong showing by the Steelers defense, who have allowed only allowed 13 points in each of their first two games, it was not enough. It’s time for our weekly look around the internet to see how the NFL world views the Steelers after their Week 2 blunder in Foxborough. FOX Sports: No.21 (No. 16 Last Week) “If that’s the way Aaron Rodgers is going to play, his last ride might be a short one. At some point, the Steelers may have to take a look at rookie Drew Allar.” – Ralph Vacchiano The Athletic: No. 21 (Last Week No.16) “The first-round tackle is only getting a couple of snaps a game, but that might change with how bad the offensive line looked Sunday. Only the Falcons are saving the Steelers from having the worst EPA in the league (minus-42.94). Fourth-round wide receiver Kaden Wetjen doesn’t have a catch yet but has made an impact as a returner. The best pick of this year’s group may be third-round quarterback Drew Allar, who made the 53-man roster but probably won’t play unless Aaron Rodgers gets hurt.” – Chad Graff and Josh Kendall CBS Sports: No.22 (Last Week No. 20) “The offense isn’t doing a lot so far this season, which has to be a concern. The defense played well enough to win at New England.” – Pete Prisco Pro Football Talk: No.18 (Last Week No. 17) “Remember when the unofficial media talking point was Mike McCarthy’s high level of attention to detail?” – Mike Florio NFL.com: No.26 (Last Week No.23) “It’s difficult to reconcile the dichotomy that currently defines the Steelers. Their defensive front is one of the most complete in football and has caused major issues for the first two offenses it has faced, yet their offense remains abysmal. Mike McCarthy’s arrival permitted Aaron Rodgers to play more aggressively, but Pittsburgh’s offensive line has regressed, the running game is nonexistent and DK Metcalf has been one of the least reliable receivers in football through two weeks. Add in Rodgers’ age and general lack of mobility under pressure (SEE: his two fumbles in Sunday’s defeat), and you have an inept unit. It’s unfair to ask the defense to carry the Steelers on a weekly basis.” – Nick Shook Yahoo! Sports: No.23 (Last Week No. 20) “The Steelers have 81 passing attempts, which is third in the league, and they’re passing about 65% of the time despite not being in pass-only mode much of the season. The Steelers never trailed by more than four points in Week 1 and the game didn’t get away from them Sunday until a Rodgers fumble was returned for a touchdown early in the fourth quarter. Mike McCarthy has just made a decision to pass it over and over like it’s 2011 with Rodgers. Pittsburgh has one offensive touchdown in eight quarters with that approach”. – Frank Schwab USA Today: No.27 (Last Week No.20) “It’s been 16 years since HC Mike McCarthy and QB Aaron Rodgers spearheaded an offense that … produced three points. It’s also been 16 years since McCarthy and Rodgers won a Super Bowl together, so …” – Nate Davis ESPN: No.25 (Last Week No. 21) “So far this season, Rodgers has completed just 8 of 24 attempts on 31 dropbacks under pressure. He has been sacked six times on such plays. Rodgers is also completing a career-low 50% against the blitz, as his off-target percentage on such throws is a career-worst 30.4%. While the offensive line’s struggles have significantly contributed to Rodgers’ inaccuracy, his decreased mobility at 42 years old has made it even more difficult to manage the pressure.” – Brooke Pryor This week’s rankings have more disparity than in recent weeks. Some outlets like CBS Sports view the Steelers about the same as they did last week, but outlets like USA Today have the Steelers ranked as the 27th best team in football. The concerns are there for the Steelers, but not everyone is hitting the panic button just yet. The Steelers have what feels like a very important home game this weekend against the 2-0 Cincinnati Bengals. Mike McCarthy and Aaron Rodgers will have their work cut out for them as the Steelers offense looks to rebound against what looks to be a vastly improved Bengals defense. full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Pittsburgh, PA, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers offensive guard Aiden Williams (78) and offensive tackle Max Iheanachor (71) participate in drills during Minicamp at UPMC Rooney Sports Complex. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Pittsburgh Steelers could be making several lineup changes along their offensive line. After a week that featured Aaron Rodgers getting sacked four times and the run game once again couldn’t get going, the Steelers appear to be working toward a new starting duo on the right side. Per Mike DeFabo of The Athletic , the offensive line combinations during practice were Zach Frazier with Brock Hoffman, Hoffman with Max Iheanachor, and then Spencer Anderson with Dylan Cook. Considering the lackluster play from the latter combination of right side offensive linemen, it’s hard to envision Hoffman and Iheanachor doing any worse than Anderson and Cook did over the course of the first two weeks. Pittsburgh faces the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 3 – a defense that is currently ninth in the NFL in pressure rate, which does not bode well for the current starting five offensive linemen. title: Steelers-Bengals preview: What to expect from Cincinnati’s offense, defense in Week 3
summary: Welcome to Week 3. The Steelers are 1-1 and, predictably, much of the past few days have been filled with doom and gloom from the fanbase. What else could we expect following a loss where the two words that could best describe the Pittsburgh offense were “haphazard” and “impotent.”  Meanwhile, the Steelers are now looking […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 20: Joe Burrow #9 of the Cincinnati Bengals huddles with teammates against the Houston Texans during the second half of the game at NRG Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to Week 3. The Steelers are 1-1 and, predictably, much of the past few days have been filled with doom and gloom from the fanbase. What else could we expect following a loss where the two words that could best describe the Pittsburgh offense were “haphazard” and “impotent.” Meanwhile, the Steelers are now looking up at division rival Cincinnati as the leaders of the AFC North. The Bengals operation through two weeks hasn’t exactly been perfect either, but after defeating the Buccaneers in a 33-27 victory in Week 1, the Bengals did just enough in Week 2 against Houston’s defense to outpace an injured Texans offense in a 20-6 win on the road. These two teams are separated in the standings by just a single game, but if you were to judge based on the vibes emanating from each respective fanbase, you’d think the Steelers were fixing to get blown out at home. Are the Bengals really the toast of the AFC North? Are the Steelers as hopeless as the internet would have you believe? Read & React takes a look: What to expect from the Bengals’ offense Rushing YPG: 95.5 (21st) Passing YPG: 213.5 (14th) PPG: 26.5 (10th) RP : The Steelers kick off division play against the Bengals, a team that Steelers fans should feel little mystery about, at least in terms of the offense. The 2020s for the Bengals offense have been defined by their quarterback, Joe Burrow, and his two superstar receivers: Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. Burrow’s health has been a major factor as well. When he’s missed time — 22 games so far since his career started in 2020 — the offense and team have struggled, winning just seven games in his absence. Burrow has been healthy thus far in 2026. He did pop up on the injury report as a limited participant during Week 2 with a back condition, but has not appeared on Week 3’s report. Entering this matchup, the Bengals are 2-0, reaching that mark for the second straight year and just the second time since Burrow’s arrival. During this era of the Bengals, the offense has largely remained the same. Burrow has lined up predominantly in shotgun for most of his career, with the Bengals heavily favoring 11 personnel (three wide receivers). According to Sumer Sports, since 2022 (the farthest back the free portion of their database goes), the Bengals have used 11 personnel sets at a 69.5% rate. That usage peaked during their 2022 Super Bowl run, when the team deployed that grouping 82.4% of the time. Regardless of the formation and personnel deployment, though, the formula has been simple: get the ball to the Italians . THIS ANGLE OF THE JA’MARR CHASE CATCH IS ONE OF THE GREATEST EVER. CHASE IS A HALL OF FAME TALENT. INSANE: pic.twitter.com/NTsidUpqo9 — MLFootball (@MLFootball) September 20, 2026 Targets Target Rate Receptions Yards Touchdowns Ja’Marr Chase 780 27.3% 529 6,924 56 Tee Higgins 626 18.3% 397 5,595 45 Oh my Tee Higgins 😮‍💨 CINvsHOU on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/VgyLDnLPsM — NFL (@NFL) September 20, 2026 If you followed the talking points coming out of Cincinnati this summer, the one big change the offense was supposed to take was a shift toward more under-center action from Burrow. Between 2022-2025, the Bengals have run plays out of shotgun at a 71% rate. An attempt to shift to more under-center stems from the desire to create both a more balanced offense and to create more explosive plays. By lining up under center, the running game should theoretically improve, as it allows the running back a longer runway to ramp up speed and to read the defense. The explosives, meanwhile, should stem from a stronger run game, as well as the offense’s ability to better disguise whether it will be running or passing the ball pre-snap, and paired with play action. So what’s the Bengals shotgun rate through two games? Try 67.2%, far from a big decrease. In Week 1, the Bengals were in shotgun 72.6% of the time. In Week 2, they shifted more towards their offseason goal (61.7% shotgun), but it was a bit of a tell, as 33 of the 36 plays from shotgun were passing plays (91.7%) and only four dropbacks occurred under center. The Bengals this offseason: "We're going to get Joe Burrow under center more! We won't run 71% of our plays from shotgun! Or have Burrow's rate of pass plays coming from the shotgun in the high 80s and above!" Through 2 weeks: 67.2% shotgun rate, 87.5% of passes from the gun pic.twitter.com/OmBHppSY74 — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) September 24, 2026 If there is one significant change the Bengals have stuck to, however, it is mixing up their personnel usage. As we mentioned earlier, the Bengals have long used 11 personnel at a high rate. While they may not be lining up under center as much as they were professing they would this summer, they have reduced their 11 personnel rate to just 53.3% through two weeks. That’s obviously a small sample size, but should be noted nonetheless. As a whole, the new trend among NFL offenses is to use less of that grouping and instead try to get more multiple tight ends on the field. The reasoning behind this once again stems from the idea of disguising what the offense is about to do. Traditionally, when multiple tight ends are on the field, that signals a run play is likely coming. Tight ends are bigger than your typical slot receiver and, in theory, should be more physically imposing, which plays into the run game. However, modern offenses are now using this accepted tendency to force defenses into playing heavier personnel (ie, linebackers), and then exploiting those defenders’ deficiencies in pass coverage to create explosive plays for the passing game. I don’t expect the Bengals to alter this shift in Week 3, especially with the team’s WR3, Andrei Iosivas out Week 3 with a thumb injury. Outside of Chase and Higgins, running back Chase Brown remains a weapon for the Steelers to be wary of. He hasn’t got it going on the ground yet this season (36-for-136 and a 3.8 YPC), but Brown is also the team’s third-leading receiver (eight receptions and 24 yards) even if the explosive plays have yet to show up there either. Last year, Brown feasted on the Steelers on the ground, rushing 29 times for 207 yards (7.1 YPC) across two games, so the defense can’t afford to write him off just because he’s had a slow start to the season. #Steelers run defense (or lack thereof) vs. Bengals (Week 7): Chase Brown had 11 carries for 108 yards (9.8 ypc). pic.twitter.com/1vrsxv798x — Tommy Jaggi (@TommyJaggi) October 17, 2025 The combination of Chase, Higgins, and Brown accounts for 40 of the Bengals’ 65 targets this season. Shutting those three down will be paramount for the Steelers defense. Beyond that trio, only tight Mike Gesicki (7) has more than four targets. Joe Burrow to Mike Gesicki for the TD and griddy 🕺 TBvsCIN on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/dJKJzKpfWG — NFL (@NFL) September 13, 2026 What to expect from the Bengals’ defense Rushing YPG Allowed: 74.5 (3rd) Passing YPG Allowed: 253.5 (27th) PPG Allowed: 16.5 (8th) RB : In past seasons, a matchup against the Bengals defense would’ve looked like a get-right game for a struggling Steelers offense. That might not be the case this year. We’re only two weeks into the season at this point, but the Bengals have a top-10 defensive unit in scoring and the league’s third-best run defense. And while it’s a little too early to victory lap any offseason moves, it’s fair to say a lot of that improvement has been thanks to the Bengals’ addition of three-time Pro Bowl nose tackle Dexter Lawrence this offseason. full_text: The Seattle Seahawks go on the road to wrap up September, going all the way from Washington state to, uh, close to Washington, DC. Landover, Maryland, to be exact. It’s the reigning Super Bowl champions against the win-less Washington Commanders in what is the home opener for Dan Quinn’s beleaguered side. Last season, Seahawks at Commanders was deemed worthy of Sunday Night Football . That ain’t happening this year, as FOX will be airing this game as a regional 10 am PT kickoff. Based on the coverage distribution outlined by the incomparable 506 Sports , Seahawks-Commanders is not going to see much attention outside of the local-ish markets. If you’re in the yellow, don’t be mellow, because Seahawks football will be on your local FOX network! Joe Davis and Greg Olsen, FOX’s No. 2 broadcast team, will be on the call for this game. Davis and Olsen worked two of the three Seahawks losses last season (vs. San Francisco 49ers, at Los Angeles Rams), as well as the 26-0 shutout of the Minnesota Vikings. While Davis and Olsen are high up the FOX charts, the distribution of this one is a measly 12 percent . Only the Arizona Cardinals at San Francisco 49ers (8 percent) is getting less attention. title: Why the Seahawks tried out two punters even though Michael Dickson is healthy
summary: The Seattle Seahawks had an interesting tryout show up on the Thursday and Friday NFL transaction wires. Just why do the Seahawks need to bring in a punter? Luke Elzinga and Colton Spangler have not been signed to the practice squad, Michael Dickson is not on the injury report, so what gives? Well the answer […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks had an interesting tryout show up on the Thursday and Friday NFL transaction wires. Just why do the Seahawks need to bring in a punter? Luke Elzinga and Colton Spangler have not been signed to the practice squad, Michael Dickson is not on the injury report, so what gives? Well the answer is simpler than it looks. Elzinga and Spangler are both left-footed punters, whereas Dickson is right-footed. The Commanders punter is Tress Way, who’s also left-footed in a league dominated by righties. San Francisco 49ers punter Corliss Waitman and Matt Araiza of the Kansas City Chiefs are also lefties, and the Seahawks will see both of them in a few weeks. There is a science behind the difference between left- and right-footed punters that was explained by Sports Illustrated’s Jenny Vrentas back in 2018 . The simple answer is that left-footed punts spin the opposite direction, counterclockwise (from the punter’s perspective), presenting an extra challenge for returners who are used to reading a right-footer’s spin. From the punt’s apex, a left-footed ball will fade to the returner’s right, whereas most returners are used to catching right-footed balls that fade to their left. That has the potential to cause a returner to hesitate or, even better for the punting team, to muff the catch. The search for answers usually ends there. That’s pretty much it. Scouting and simulating playing a left-footed punter is the goal for Seattle. They did this last season before playing the New Orleans Saints and their punter, Kai Kroeger. Seahawks tried out another left-footed punter. Seem committed to having one on practice squad next week in preparation for playing the Saints. https://t.co/Uffk8SVuPA — Bob Condotta (@bcondotta) September 12, 2025 Chasing edges also means leaving no stone unturned. No need to read too much into Seattle’s punter tryouts beyond needing some lefties to prepare for several leftie punters over the next month.

title: Seahawks-Commanders game designations: Sam Darnold will play, Julian Love ruled out
summary: The Seattle Seahawks will have Sam Darnold back in the lineup, but they’ll be down both of their starting safeties against the Washington Commanders. Mike Macdonald confirmed on Friday that Darnold is not on the final injury report and will start on Sunday. He missed almost all of the Week 1 opener against the New […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks will have Sam Darnold back in the lineup, but they’ll be down both of their starting safeties against the Washington Commanders. Mike Macdonald confirmed on Friday that Darnold is not on the final injury report and will start on Sunday. He missed almost all of the Week 1 opener against the New England Patriots and all of Week 2 versus the Arizona Cardinals with a glute injury. His injury (and, consequently, his initial timeline) was unclear, but he’s made significant strides in his recovery and is all set to go. Drew Lock will once again be the backup quarterback after two great showings, and Jalen Milroe will presumably be the emergency third quarterback. Here’s the bad news: Seattle’s safety injuries are piling up. Julian Love’s calf tightened up in practice, and the Seahawks have held him out of this weekend’s game. Love, who missed half of last regular season due to injury, has been off to an outstanding start to 2026, recording interceptions in both games. Ty Okada’s hamstring still hasn’t healed up, which means the Seahawks’ starting safety tandem will be Rodney Thomas II and A.J. Finley . Seattle will presumably look at elevating at least one of Maxen Hook or D’Anthony Bell from the practice squad on Saturday. Nose tackle Brandon Pili is questionable with a concussion and neck injury, but he’s the only other player with an injury designation. Seattle’s injury situation is decidedly tame compared to what the Commanders are dealing with. Guard Sam Cosmi will be out after Kaytron Allen ran into him and knocked him out of the Dallas Cowboys game. Tight end Chig Okonkwo is also out, as is starting linebacker Frankie Luvu, and starting safety Nick Cross.

title: A Seahawks All-22 review of the good and bad from Week 2 win vs. Cardinals
summary: Sam Darnold remained sidelined, Drew Lock was making his first start for the Seattle Seahawks since 2023, and the Arizona Cardinals were coming off an unexpected road win over the Los Angeles Chargers. On top of that, playing in Arizona has historically been anything but straightforward for the Seahawks. The game was still tied 7-7 […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - SEPTEMBER 20: Drew Lock #2 of the Seattle Seahawks throws as Jack Gibbens #50 of the Arizona Cardinals defends during the third quarter of the game at State Farm Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sam Darnold remained sidelined, Drew Lock was making his first start for the Seattle Seahawks since 2023, and the Arizona Cardinals were coming off an unexpected road win over the Los Angeles Chargers. On top of that, playing in Arizona has historically been anything but straightforward for the Seahawks. The game was still tied 7-7 heading into halftime. However, once again, Seattle made the necessary adjustments after the break and took complete control of the game. Lock completed 19 of 26 passes for 235 yards and three touchdowns, while Jaxon Smith-Njigba turned in one of the best games of his career with nine catches for 155 yards and three touchdowns. But the final score doesn’t mean everything on tape was perfect. There were still questionable decisions, missed opportunities and moments when Seattle’s execution wasn’t where it needs to be. The good news is that the Seahawks were able to overcome those mistakes — and, unlike Week 1, they eventually pulled away instead of having to survive until the final possession. So let’s get into the good and bad from Seattle’s Week 2 win over Arizona. The Bad Red-zone play calling Brian Fleury had a good game overall, and there were plenty of good play calls that I’ll highlight later in this article. But his approach near the goal line wasn’t quite as creative at times. For a team like Seattle, which wants to build its identity around offensive efficiency and a strong defense, red-zone execution is critical. I have no problem running the ball four straight times when you’re that close to the goal line. Even knowing you have the reigning OPOY and that he probably deserved at least one target, I understand the decision to stay committed to the run. The problem was how predictable Seattle became across those eight runs. One drive eventually ended with a turnover on downs and the other ended in the AJ Barner quarterback sneak, but Arizona was able to anticipate what Seattle wanted to do on several of those snaps. There were also a couple of lazy-looking screens to George Holani and Rashid Shaheed that didn’t do much to stress the defense. This is the kind of thing that becomes more important against better defenses. Seattle doesn’t need to abandon what it does well near the goal line, but it does need to make sure defenses can’t sit on the most obvious answer. There were some good concepts in this game. The problem is that the red-zone portion of the playbook didn’t always show the same creativity. That’s something worth keeping an eye on as the season progresses. Offensive line communication/execution The offensive line had a good game overall, and it’s important to make that clear before getting into the problems. Seattle ran for 162 yards, protected Lock reasonably well and eventually took control of the line of scrimmage. The fourth-quarter drive in particular was a showcase of the physical advantage Seattle’s offensive line was able to create. And as a Seahawks fan, seeing John Benton receive the game ball in the locker room was pretty awesome. But there were still a few snaps where the communication and synchronization broke down, both in the passing game and the running game. Here’s an example of a communication error. Here’s a communication error.The OL slides right, but Holani and Sundell both block the same defender. Sundell should pick up No. 50 while Holani works into the A-gap, leaving a free path to Lock.Lock still makes a great throw under pressure, but the OL mistake is there. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-25T02:25:08.816Z The offensive line appears to be sliding to the right, and there is a mistake between George Holani and Jalen Sundell. My read is that Sundell should have slid to pick up No. 50, with Holani working directly into the A-gap. Instead, both players end up blocking the same defender. That leaves the linebacker with a free path to Drew Lock. Lock still delivers a great pass under pressure, despite not having a stable base when he throws it. This is exactly the kind of snap where the quarterback can cover for an offensive-line mistake. But the mistake is still there. Here’s another example of an execution issue. Another execution issue.Seattle uses 7OL and 2TEs, with Olu as the FB and Josh Jones as 6th OL. The idea is good, but Zabel gets tangled pulling, while Olu can’t adjust after Lucas gets pushed back.I believe the intended gap is between Olu, Zabel and the TE. Execution kills the play on 4th down. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-25T02:26:35.092Z Seattle comes out with seven offensive linemen and two tight ends, which is about as clear a signal as you can get that this is going to be a run. Olu Oluwatimi is lined up as the fullback, while Josh Jones is serving as the sixth offensive lineman. The idea is good, but Grey Zabel gets tangled up trying to pull, and Olu can’t adjust once the play starts developing, particularly after Abe Lucas gets pushed backward. I believe the intended path is the gap between Olu, Zabel and the tight end. Because of the execution issue, Seattle fails to convert on fourth down. These are small details, but they matter. The offensive line was physically winning plenty of reps against Arizona. The next step is making sure everyone is seeing and executing the same picture on every snap. Rashid Shaheed is starting the year well below expectations Rashid Shaheed hasn’t exactly had the start to the season many expected. After a quiet performance against New England, Shaheed finished the Arizona game with three catches for 35 yards on six targets, plus one carry for four yards. And I’m going to be honest: those numbers are better than the game he actually played. Since the Patriots game, Shaheed has looked a little sluggish as a returner, a long way from the explosive dynamism he showed last season. Shaheed has looked sluggish as a returner since New England, far from last year’s explosiveness.That continued vs. Arizona, where a fumble early in the second half could’ve changed a tied game. Chazz Surratt bailed him out, returning it to ARI’s 40.And yes, Surratt was a QB at North Carolina — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-25T02:28:50.289Z That continued against the Cardinals and culminated in a fumble early in the second half that could have changed the story of a game that was tied at that point. Chazz Surratt bailed out the wide receiver. And, in true old-school quarterback fashion — yes, Surratt was a quarterback at North Carolina early in his college career — he took off running and got Seattle all the way to its Cardinal’s 40-yard line. That’s a nice way to redeem himself after the penalty against New England. Shaheed’s bigger issue is as a route runner. summary: In Week 2 the Seattle Seahawks handily defeated the Arizona Cardinals to keep pace with the San Francisco 49ers atop the division. The Niners, of course, opened the season by defeating the offseason champion Los Angeles Rams, giving San Francisco fans hopes as a schedule that is relatively soft outside of the quickly-approaching divisional matchup […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 10: Defensive end Nick Bosa #97 of the San Francisco 49ers battles with offensive tackle Stone Forsythe #78 of the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on October 10, 2024 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Robin Alam/ISI Photos/Getty Images) | Getty Images In Week 2 the Seattle Seahawks handily defeated the Arizona Cardinals to keep pace with the San Francisco 49ers atop the division. The Niners, of course, opened the season by defeating the offseason champion Los Angeles Rams, giving San Francisco fans hopes as a schedule that is relatively soft outside of the quickly-approaching divisional matchup against Seattle in Week 5. However, according to a report from NFL insider Adam Schefter of ESPN, the Niners may be without a key member of their defense for the next few weeks, including the Week 5 matchup against the Seahawks, after Nick Bosa suffered a calf injury during practice Thursday. Five-time Pro-Bowl DE Nick Bosa pulled his calf during Thursday’s practice and now is expected to miss “a few weeks”, including Sunday’s game vs. the Cardinals, sources tell me and @RapSheet . The team is figuring out whether or not Bosa needs to be placed on injured reserve. pic.twitter.com/eQIb7JBKut — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) September 25, 2026 Bosa is, obviously, among the most experienced and decorated members of a Niners defensive front that has been beset by injuries so far this year. San Francisco currently has six members of the defensive front seven on injured reserve, including five defensive linemen in C.J. West, Sam Okuayinonu, Mikail Kamara, Andrew Famer II and Alfred Collins. If Bosa does land on injured reserve ahead of the 49ers game against the Cardinals on Sunday, it would keep him out through Week 7, with San Francisco having a bye in Week 8.

full_text: Last week, we talked about how Jadarian Price was essentially the only rookie worth focusing on in this series. Somehow, that changed pretty quickly. Against the Arizona Cardinals, the Seattle Seahawks went from 24 rookie snaps in Week 1 to 53 in Week 2, with Price continuing to see a significant role while fifth-round guard Beau Stephens made his NFL debut. Julian Neal also saw a couple of defensive snaps late in the game, while Avery Smith continued to contribute on special teams. Let’s analyze some of the key plays from this game! All data used in this article was taken from PFF. Jadarian Price, Running Back (24 snaps) Price left the game with a chest injury that, at least initially, did not appear to be serious. Had he stayed healthy, there’s a good chance he would have surpassed his career-high on Notre Dame of 15 touches. Instead, he finished with 14: 13 carries for 52 yards and one reception for eight yards. The numbers were solid, especially considering he also had a 25-yard run, but the tape showed both why Seattle was willing to give him a significant workload and why there is still plenty for him to clean up. Price’s ball-security concerns weren’t just pre-draft noise at Notre Dame. He had a tendency to carry the ball high through contact, leaving it exposed.That shows up here. Watch the previous snap, too—the same issue is visible. This is something Seattle needs to keep emphasizing. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-24T20:17:11.659Z Let’s start with the obvious one. A lot of the pre-draft discussion around Price’s fumbles seemed to downplay the issue, but it was a real concern during his time at Notre Dame. Price has a tendency to carry the ball relatively high when he enters contact, leaving it exposed and giving defenders an opportunity to attack it. That’s exactly what happens here. And if you watch the snap immediately before the fumble, you can see a similar issue with ball security. The technique hasn’t disappeared just because he got to the NFL. This is something Seattle will need to continue emphasizing with him, particularly as his workload increases. I really liked this snap coming right after the fumble.Price responded with confidence. He makes his cut, lowers his shoulder, takes the contact and squeezes out extra yards.For a rookie coming off his first NFL fumble, that immediate response says a lot about his confidence. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-24T20:18:51.937Z I really liked this snap coming immediately after the fumble. Price wasn’t put in the doghouse after the mistake. Instead, Seattle went right back to him, and he immediately showed that the turnover wasn’t going to change how he approached the game. He makes his cut, doesn’t try to avoid contact, lowers his shoulder and still manages to squeeze out a few extra yards. For a rookie coming directly off his first NFL fumble, there is something to be said about responding this way. Here’s another area where Price can improve.Seattle runs a long trap with Grey Zabel pulling. Price’s aiming point should be the guard’s left shoulder, but he hesitates when the path isn’t clean and briefly considers bouncing outside before cutting back in.Those extra steps cost him some burst. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-24T20:19:44.318Z Here’s another area where Price has room to improve. Seattle runs a long trap here, with Grey Zabel pulling. I believe Price’s aiming point should be the left shoulder of the guard. Instead, Price sees that the initial path isn’t completely clean, hesitates and briefly considers bouncing the run outside before cutting back inside. Those extra steps cost him some of his initial burst. Price takes an extra lateral step before cutting. His acceleration still gets him positive yardage, but that wasted movement matters.At the NFL level, hesitation can turn a 4-yard gain into a much bigger run. He’s still learning to trust his reads and get north faster. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-24T20:21:12.121Z This snap makes the issue even clearer. Price takes one additional lateral step before making his cut. He still gets positive yardage because of his acceleration, but the wasted movement is noticeable. This is the kind of thing that can be easy to overlook because the play still gains positive yardage, but at the NFL level, those hesitation steps can be the difference between a four-yard gain and a much bigger run. And, again, this is not unusual for a rookie. Price is still learning how quickly he needs to commit to his reads at this level. Once he becomes more decisive with his initial read and gets north faster, there’s a good chance these runs start producing significantly more yardage. Here, Price is much more decisive. He doesn’t waste any steps, makes a clean cut and immediately attacks the edge with his explosiveness. This probably ends in a touchdown if he doesn’t slip. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-24T20:22:07.818Z Here, Price is much more decisive. He makes his read, cuts outside with clean tech and immediately puts his speed and explosiveness on display as he attacks the edge. This probably ends up as a touchdown if he doesn’t slip. Price’s best play so far.He patiently lets the FB and RT blocks develop, sees the RT lose inside, then explodes through the opening and attacks the edge for 25 yards. Great balance after contact, too.And excellent block by JSN here. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-24T20:23:50.282Z This was probably Price’s best play until now. It’s a 25-yard run, but what stands out isn’t simply the final result. Price does a good job reading the development of the blocks from the fullback and right tackle, allowing the blocks to develop instead of immediately committing to the first available gap. He waits for the right moment, see that RT is losing inside then explodes through the opening and attacks the edge. He also shows good balance after the first tackle attempt, keeping himself upright and continuing to gain yards staying on the field. This is the version of Price Seattle wants to see more consistently. The explosiveness is already there. The next step is making the reads and decisions that allow him to access that explosiveness more often. And, as a quick aside: excellent block by JSN here. Bud Clark, Defensive Back (0 snaps) IR. Julian Neal, Cornerback (2 snaps) Neal finally got onto the field, although only during garbage time on Arizona’s final drive. Julian Neal first NFL tackle — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-24T20:28:28.877Z He played two defensive snaps and recorded his first defensive tackle as a Seahawk. There isn’t much to evaluate from such a small sample, but getting those first regular-season snaps out of the way is still part of the process for a rookie who has spent most of his time only on special teams. Beau Stephens, Guard (27 snaps) This was the surprise of the rookie class from a playing-time perspective. Stephens played 27 snaps in his NFL debut, while Christian Haynes handled 43. Mike Macdonald clarified that this wasn’t necessarily a planned rotation between the two guards, but Seattle still found a way to get Stephens meaningful playing time. With Anthony Bradford now on injured reserve , those 27 snaps could prove especially important as the Seahawks figure out what they have in the rookie. With Anthony Bradford now on injured reserve and expected to miss at least four games, those snaps could become extremely important for Stephens. Beau loses the initial hand battle against Josh Sweat and never establishes himself in the rep. His feet also need to be quicker here.The positive: Stephens keeps fighting after losing early, helping Lock escape the pressure.Also, good lord, what a terrible drop by Shaheed. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-09-24T20:24:58.937Z This was a pressure allowed by Beau. He lines up against EDGE Josh Sweat and loses the initial hand battle, failing to establish himself in the rep. His feet also need to move…

title: Seahawks vs. Commanders predictions: Expect another big game from Seattle’s rushing attack
summary: The Seattle Seahawks enters Week 3 with a 2-0 record and will travel to Maryland to take on the Washington Commanders and try and extend their winning streak to 13 games. The Seahawks are currently 7.5-point favorites at FanDuel Sportsbook, with the total set at 40.5 points. This matchup looks considerably different than it did […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - SEPTEMBER 20: Jadarian Price #8 of the Seattle Seahawks rushes the football against the Arizona Cardinals during the NFL game at State Farm Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. The Seahawks defeated the Cardinals 31-7. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seattle Seahawks enters Week 3 with a 2-0 record and will travel to Maryland to take on the Washington Commanders and try and extend their winning streak to 13 games. The Seahawks are currently 7.5-point favorites at FanDuel Sportsbook , with the total set at 40.5 points. This matchup looks considerably different than it did when the lines first opened. Washington is 0-2 after losing 37-20 to Dallas and will be without Jayden Daniels, while Seattle is still waiting to determine whether Sam Darnold will return from his injury. That uncertainty makes quarterback-specific bets less appealing for now. Instead, there are several other markets that stand out, particularly with Seattle’s rushing attack and its defense. Here are four predictions for Seahawks-Commanders. 1. Jadarian Price scores a touchdown Jadarian Price’s status is one of the things to monitor before kickoff, but if the rookie is active, I like his chances of finding the end zone. Price left Seattle’s 31-7 victory over Arizona with a chest injury, although his initial X-rays were negative. He was limited in practice, keeping the door open for him to play against Washington. Price has already shown why Seattle invested a first-round pick in him. Price had 52 rushing yards on 10 carries against New England in Week 1 before adding 52 yards on 13 carries against Arizona, including a 25-yard run. Prediction: Jadarian Price anytime touchdown scorer 2. Jaxon Smith-Njigba goes over 90 receiving yards At this point, there isn’t much reason to stop expecting big numbers from Jaxon Smith-Njigba. JSN has 17 receptions for 277 yards and four touchdowns through two games, including a three-touchdown performance against Arizona. He has quickly become the focal point of Seattle’s passing game, regardless of who is playing quarterback. The bigger question is whether Washington can find a way to slow him down. The Commanders enter this game after allowing 37 points to Dallas, while Seattle’s offense has already shown it can generate explosive plays through multiple areas of the field. Seattle could also have opportunities to attack through the air if Washington commits extra defenders to stopping the run. The one concern is game script. If Seattle controls the game early, there may not be enough passing volume for JSN to approach another 150-yard performance. Still, his role makes 90 yards a reasonable target. Prediction: Jaxon Smith-Njigba over 90 receiving yards 3. Seahawks cover -7.5 The current FanDuel line has Seattle favored by 7.5 points. That is a larger number than the Seahawks have had to cover in either of their first two games, but there are reasons to believe Seattle can create enough separation. The Seahawks have outscored their opponents 44-17 through two games. The defense has been the team’s biggest constant, while the offense has found ways to produce despite the uncertainty at quarterback. Washington, meanwhile, is 0-2 and will have to adjust to playing without Daniels. Marcus Mariota will take over at quarterback, changing the way the Commanders can attack Seattle’s defense. The biggest concern with laying 7.5 points is Seattle’s offensive ceiling if the quarterback situation remains unsettled. But the Seahawks don’t necessarily need another 30-point performance to cover. If Seattle establishes its rushing attack and controls the clock, a two-score victory is within reach. Prediction: Seahawks -7.5 4. Under 40.5 total points The total is currently set at 40.5 points at FanDuel. This might seem strange after Seattle scored 31 points last week, but the Seahawks have yet to play a game that went over this number. Their defense has also allowed just 17 points through the first two weeks. Washington has gone in the opposite direction, with both of its games going over the closing total. But the Commanders will now have to play without Daniels, potentially changing the way they approach the game offensively. Without their starting quarterback, Washington could lean more heavily on the running game and shorter throws rather than asking Mariota to consistently attack downfield against Seattle’s defense. Seattle could also become more run-heavy if it builds a lead, which would help shorten the game and reduce the number of possessions available to both teams. A game finishing somewhere in the 20s for Seattle and the 10s for Washington would comfortably stay below the current number. Prediction: Under 40.5 points Final score prediction The biggest variable remains Seattle’s quarterback situation, but the Seahawks have enough talent around the position to make that uncertainty less important than it might appear. Seattle should be able to establish its rushing attack against Washington, while its defense has the matchup to make life difficult for a Commanders offense without Daniels. I expect Washington to keep things competitive early, but Seattle should pull away in the second half. Seahawks 24, Commanders 13 That gives Seattle an 11-point victory, enough to cover the current 7.5-point spread while keeping the game below the 40.5-point total. 12s, make your voices heard on the SB Nation app!
